MR. RYNARD-DELAYS IN ANSWERING STARRED QUESTIONS
speechtext:
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I want to draw to your attention one of the failings of this House, namely, the failure to deal with the starred questions. It was almost four years ago, the length of this parliament, when I first brought this to your attention. A starred question had been on the order paper for a period of just about one month.
I will put it in order of sequence. On February 27, 1975, I rose in the House of Commons to inquire about a question which was of importance to me. At that particular time a starred question of mine had been on the order paper for approximately four weeks and had not been answered. I naturally assumed that that question would be answered within a week, as was the custom when I first came to the House of Commons. As custom dictated the law of proceedings in the House, I accepted this to be so.
When I rose on this point of order, Mr. Speaker, you stated that I had raised a very interesting point but you could not find any authority which would entitle a member to an answer to a starred question within a certain period of time. What it did entitle me to, of course, was an oral answer in the House of Commons when that answer was given. As I have stated, this was not my interpretation of the starred question. Indeed, I felt it was accepted fact that starred questions were to be answered within a week, or the minister contacted that individual who had asked the question.
In the Mother of Parliaments, a member who desires an oral answer to his question must distinguish it with an asterisk, and notice of any such question must appear on the order paper
4204

April 6, 1978
Point of Order-Mr. Rynard
two days before that on which an answer is desired, except that questions received before 2:30 p.m. on Mondays and Tuesdays may be put down for oral answer on the following Monday and Thursday respectively.
As a matter of historical interest, Mr. Speaker, the starred question came into being in 1910 when Sir Wilfrid Laurier was Prime Minister of Canada. At that time he stated that many questions are put on the floor of the House that have no interest except to the individual putting the questions, but if a member desired to have an oral answer he had only to put an asterisk to his question and it would come before the House at once. In 1910 the rules of the House provided only for written questions, but members persisted in asking oral questions and, by custom, this became a rule. The starred question was introduced in an attempt to reduce the emphasis on oral questions. Oral questions were not recognized by the rules of this House, as far as I can find out, until 1964.
In 1955 the Special Committee on Procedure sought to establish more firmly the existence of the starred question, which was then given a special place on the order paper on one day of the week. No member was allowed to have more than three starred questions on the order paper at any one time, and this is still the accepted practice. This, of course, was the situation when I first entered the House of Commons.
The very thing that has happened today is that the order paper has become so full of questions that the backlog goes far beyond the original interest of those starred questions being answered within a few days. It appears to me to be a very foolish thing, and a waste of time and printing, when one finds at the end of a parliament that hundreds of these questions remain unanswered long months after they had been placed on the order paper.
As a matter of fact, John B. Stewart, in his work on procedure in the House of Commons, offers an unique explanation for the existence of starred questions, by stating that usually the purpose-and this is very fundamental to our democracy-is to ensure that the House and the press will not remain oblivious to any horrendous information elicited about extravagance, patronage, or mismanagement by government itself. This strikes at the roots of democracy, and it is the right of the people to know.
I want to thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your advice in the House and for your request, on more than one occasion, that the Special Committee on Procedure meet to deal with this matter.
I am further upset that this infringes on the rights and privileges of a new member particularly, who might have difficulty in the wording of his oral question. Further, I see no reason why the committee should repeatedly ignore the request of the Speaker who, all of us feel, has the toughest job in this House. Not only must he have the ability to think and the wisdom to guide, but his own conscience is on trial. As well, of course, as ignoring my own personal request as a member of this House on several occasions, and the refusal of the head of that committee to meet, I do not believe that this would be the wish of this government or of any member of the opposition.

subtopic: MR. RYNARD-DELAYS IN ANSWERING STARRED QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I just add a few words in support of my colleague with regard to starred questions. Governments in the past have been absolutely contemptuous of members with respect to the nature of starred questions which, by tradition, practice, and ordinary decent consideration, have been earmarked for early attention by the House and could not be sloughed off as a matter to be made an order for return. The fact that starred questions exist today does not mean a thing.
I have intervened not only to support my colleague and others who want to use starred questions, but in order to support you, Mr. Speaker, in your stand, and to lay the blame where it belongs.
I am vice-chairman of the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization. I want to put on record that the committee has not met once during this past session except for the formal organizational meeting. Not only in this session but in the long prior session, the government House leader has refused consistently to refer one item of House rules to that committee. This matter should be taken into account by the committee itself. The government House leader has been contemptuous of this House where there was an agreement on both sides that certain modifications should take place. The House has been run as his personal fiefdom when he is here and, when he is not, it is totally neglected.
I do not know how we are going to cut the Gordian knot. Shall we have to decide that the committee will take up matters without reference from the House and bring in their return? Something has to be done, Mr. Speaker. For the three terms that I have been vice-president of the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization, the present government House leader, not only in this parliament but in a previous parliament, has consistently refused to refer any particular point to the committee, with the result that nothing is done. We have this continuing abuse, and we have anomalies in practice. The duties of Mr. Speaker are made more difficult, and the functions of members are made equally difficult.
I insist again that the blame lies entirely with the government House leader who has refused to refer these matters to the committee.

Mr. Speaker, I think we must still put the facts in their proper perspective. What the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) says is not quite accurate. As I remember very well, since I was myself a member of the Committee on Procedure and Organization, two years ago, at least three very detailed reports on parliamentary reform were prepared and discussed by this committee. The committee even sat during the summer recess. We came here to Ottawa, and what stopped the House from adopting those reports which recommended reforms and important changes was that the parties had undertaken to submit those reports to their respective caucuses. The Progressive Conservative party never did accept to ratify those important changes, which were liberal to say the least and which would have greatly helped modernize
April 6, 1978

the House and make it more efficient. This was therefore the true reason. It was not obstruction on the part of the government House leader, but the fact that the Progressive Conservative members of parliament did not come to an agreement about the changes which had been discussed and which had obtained the approval of the members of the committee. This is the real reason.
As for the suggestion of the member who spoke before the hon. member for Edmonton West concerning starred questions, I think that it is very interesting and should be examined in due time by the Committee on Procedure and Organization, but I think we should not examine only this matter but consider also a global reform. We must not forget, Mr. Speaker, that during the past year and a half, or rather the past year, the main reform in this institution has been the televising of our debates. God knows that hon. members have co-operated under your able leadership to enable this reform to be made as smoothly and as efficiently as possible. Now that our debates are televised, I am convinced that an in-depth reform of parliamentary procedure will follow and that very shortly, probably in the early days of the thirty-first parliament, the Committee on Procedure and Organization will be able to study many changes to parliamentary procedures and that this will quite probably include the starred questions mentioned by the hon. member.
For our part, I want to assure the House that we are open to all changes which aim at making this parliament more modern, more efficient and more respectful of the rights of members of parliament and the population as a whole.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Wednesday, April 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chretien that Bill C-18, to amend the Anti-Inflation Act and guidelines, be read the third time and do pass.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT AMENDMENT TO EXTEND RANGE OF PERSONS TO WHOM ANTI-INFLATION GUIDELINES APPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is some five years since I first spoke in this House with regard to the subject of wage and price controls. I recall the circumstances in 1972 at the time of the budget being presented by the former member for Ottawa-Carleton. Inflation was start-

ing to show its head, following what I consider to be the most disastrous budget that hon. gentleman ever presented in so far as the country was concerned. We are still reaping the whirlwind of it, as well as the slack money policy which accompanied that budget of 1972. It was an election year budget that was full of goodies.
It is conceivable that in its desperation for what is going to be an electoral campaign in a short time, this government, bankrupt of policy and bankrupt of effective action, will come down with a budget that is going to insert into the Canadian economy long-range nefarious effects, as was done in 1972.
At that time I spoke about the need of an effective wage and price control policy. This was continued as the policy of our party. My colleague from Don Valley spoke at length on that occasion with regard to the proposal, and others of my colleagues supported it.
This was not something that was suddenly dreamed up on the eve of the election in 1974. It had been a considered policy. It had been strongly advocated by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), who was then Leader of the Opposition. It was a good program as enunciated by him.
One of the problems in 1974 was that in a spirit of dishonesty, in light of subsequent events, a government spokesman decried and belaboured the wage policy. The New Democratic Party followed suit. In Ontario, and that is where it happened, they convinced the voters that they should have nothing to do with an incomes policy. The Leader of the NDP came along immediately after he had done what he thought was effective on the Conservative party policy, and came down with a prices review board, just prices. Of course, his program was soon picked apart. His followers quite rightly read into the program that it was another form of incomes policy. It was to control prices and profits, but somehow or other not wages. There is no way to control prices and profits without controlling wages and rents.
I have the record here if anyone wants to see the onslaught of inflation over the years. In 1971 the government changed the base to 100 from what it had previously been since 1963. Taking the 1971 base of 100, when we go back to 1966, it only took 83 cents to produce what in 1971 cost $1.
In 1975 there apparently was a series of events which led to the resignation of the minister of finance and, on the eve of the re-opening of parliament, the institution of a wage and price controls program that is now to terminate on April 14. The legislation today deals with that.
Let us see what the record has been since 1971. In 1971 it was 100. In 1972 it was 104.8. In 1973, after that infamous budget of 1972, it went to 112.7. In 1974 the people were still not conscious of inflation. They had not suffered enough. It went to 125, in other words 12.3 points on all items.

three years as we are now going to have. What was needed was a psychological shock to the minds of the public, and to bring to the attention of governments at all levels that this business of charging what the market would bear, passing costs on to anybody, instituting a cushion and deluding the public that inflation was not here and that it was something which could be swept under the rug, was not acceptable. People on low fixed incomes, people receiving unemployment benefits, and people who had their own savings and the savings of generations, were finding that their money was being eaten away by inflation. These people, as well as people living on savings from insurance policies, were being offered as sacrificial lambs on the altar of inflation. There was total inaction in the face of inflation.
In July of 1969 the Prime Minister appeared on television to deal with inflation as it stood then. At that time we were dealing with an inflation rate of about 5 per cent or 6 per cent, which was peanuts compared with today. We would be in a seventh heaven today if we could get inflation down to say, 5 per cent. Then later came the statement that the government had wrestled inflation to the ground. What nonsense! The man was completely deluding the Canadian public. As a lawyer I would almost say that he was crassly ignorant or grossly negligent in saying that to the Canadian public, and then instituting programs such as indexing of old age pensions and civil service pensions. Those measures were designed as a temporary cushion. They were palliatives, but inflation was not cured. The government did nothing about curing inflation.
In 1972 we saw full indexing of old age security, public service pensions, RCMP pensions and, after a certain point, armed services superannuation. That was when we had the cheap money policy. There was an increase in monetary supply.
I invite hon. members to read the speech made last Monday by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). I invite the public to read that speech. It was a long speech, but it covered chapter after chapter of inaction. It was an exhaustive review of bad economic policy and bad economic actions by this government. However, from 1972 on we had those palliatives.
It was almost like telling someone, "Yes, we realize that you have rotten teeth, that you need some work on the roots of some of your teeth and that they hurt," and then offering some aspirin or some other type of medication. It was like telling that person to take two tablets a day to relieve the pain, that the prescription could be renewed and that if the pain remained, the dosage could be increased. Nothing was said about getting to the root cause of the problem, the decay in the roots of the teeth. In the same way, no one on the government side looked to the cause of the decay in the economy.
How on earth can an administration continue to support double digit inflation and ever-increasing unemployment? In those days half a million people were unemployed, and there were all-party debates here about that. The New Democratic Party put resolution after resolution on the order paper. After two and a half years of wage and price controls we still have indexation. There has been an increase in the frequency of indexation, and now there are one million unemployed. Where are we with regard to inflation? In January of 1978 it had reached 167.8. In other words, compared with the dollar of 1971, seven years ago-and seven years is a short time in the economic life of the country-it now costs two thirds more to buy the same quantity of goods and services. We wonder why people outside this country are concerned about the falling value of the Canadian dollar. There is the answer, Mr. Speaker. Our Canadian dollar is a true reflection of the economic performance in this country during the last decade.
If my good friend, the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Railton), would like to take a look at the tables in the Bank of Canada's monthly review at page 62, I would invite him to read for his edification and education something that he should know. I am sure that his wife tells him that in the past decade it has cost 78 per cent more to buy $1 worth of goods and services. Does the hon. member pretend that that is the right conduct of the economic affairs of this country? What does he think will have to be the course of action over the next decade if that was the performance over the last one? If you take another 68 per cent or 78 per cent increase on this total, in other words, if you take 78 per cent of 178 per cent, as the hon. gentleman knows, we will have an increase of 100 per cent, so we will get 350 per cent. There had to be an amendment, and that is true in the legal sense, because it was clearly the intention indicated by a number of people that if there were in existence unexpired multiple year contracts at the time of the expiry of the anti-inflation legislation, when the controls came off not only would any full year's provision in the contract be applicable, but any amount in the roll-back would immediately spring up and be due to the workers under the collective agreement. That would make utter nonsense of any AIB roll-back or any order by the administrator. That is provided for in section 48, and I am glad to see it there. There are also provisions in section 47 specifying that notwithstanding any order of the AIB or the administrator, when the controls came off, the wage rates provided for in the contract would become binding, and naturally there would be considerable increases in the arrears.

The study of this bill in committee provided a classic example of how a very complicated subject cannot get adequate treatment. In the committee structure, an hon. member is given ten minutes. A committee session consists of approximately 80 to 85 minutes. In the first round, members are given ten minutes, and in the second round they are given five minutes. That may continue on, but there were only three sessions on this matter. The minister was not very, very forthcoming. He would not give information. The net result is that what you are attempting to find out in committee is withheld. There was pressure, and then the study and the legislation were terminated.
As a matter of fact, perhaps this is the bill the Minister of Finance refused to come back to committee with, unless certain things happened in the House. I was not present for that, but indeed it is a strange attitude to exhibit. I have no apology to make, and I reject any suggestions that speeches made by myself and my colleagues will take some time. We are here for the purposes of making a review. I am taking my allotted time. I was not involved in the committee, so I will canvass the subject as I see it.
I disagreed with the chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board concerning a particular case which came to my attention. There was an exchange of correspondence. The anti-inflation program does a grave disservice to a firm which is operated efficiently. I am referring to a particular trucking firm in western Canada. That firm increased its profits beyond those of the base year, as defined by the Anti-Inflation Board. It was not done by reason of any increase in rates. It was done by re-organization in certain parts, and greater efficiency.
When the AIB examined the profits of this company, it indicated that they were over 95 per cent of the base year or the compliance period. Therefore, the board indicated that there would have to be a return of the excess profits to the patrons. That is totally impractical and impossible, unless the company reduced its present rates thereby putting out of business other smaller competitors. If that occurred, of course it would pick up more business, and a self-defeating cycle would occur. Instead, the company proposed to take the surplus profits and invest them in better capital facilities, rather than distributing them as dividends or for the payment of higher executive salaries. I protested this. There was no way this could be accepted by the board as an economic principle.
I received a letter dated September 30, 1977, from the Chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board. In part it reads as follows:
I agree with your statement that the program "in many ways" discourages attempts by management and employees to improve efficiency in that, by and large, we require the benefits from such actions to be passed on to the marketplace. Indeed, it is difficult for me to imagine an anti-inflation program which did not require such a contribution from the more efficient firms. At the same time, it must be recognized that this policy only impacts on the companies that are operating close to their target profit levels.
It is extraordinarily difficult to justify that the achievers, either through improvement in management or performance by employees, must be penalized. This is what happened
Anti-Inflation Act
precisely in this particular case. The case is under review before the administrator, and I trust we will see a reversal of the AIB decision.
Before finishing, I should like to indicate that the other day I heard a very intriguing radio program on the CBC. Some time in the past there was quite an uproar in the media when the salary figure of the president of Canadian Pacific Railway was published. It had been obtained in Washington. Of course it was in the $300,000 range. People booed and hawed. They made various asinine and inane comments about it, not realizing that most of it goes toward income tax.
A former member of the press gallery, who is now stationed in Washington, went to the appropriate government agency, and under their right to know legislation, he was able to unearth the exact salary figures of leaders in the Canadian labour movement who occupy executive positions in international unions. The results were very interesting. I will not refer to any particular example, but some of these people were earning over $100,000. I should like to hear the comments of the hon. members of the New Democratic Party, particularly those who feel anyone earning over $15,000 is somehow robbing his employer. What about these people?
If it is conceivable and correct that the salaries of public officers, such as of the Prime Minister, cabinet ministers, and of Your Honour, shall be public knowledge, then the law should apply to everyone. We have a right to know. There is a great deal being said about that. The United States does not seem to be suffering from its right to know legislation. Under that legislation, corporations must file the salaries and allowances of their corporate officers, or the schedule of salaries of executive officers and directors must be filed with the Security Exchange Commission. One can get at that information in the United States, but in Canada it is impossible to do that. Similar legislation with regard to labour unions, because they are executives of major economic units, is in force in the United States. They are required to file the exact figure of their salaries, down to the last dollar and cent.
I think it is only fair, and it is my personal suggestion that if elected officials must post their salaries, as do certain other officers and directors of public companies, then it is right and just that those people in private corporations who are officers and directors, and executives of labour unions, should file their incomes. It should be out in the open where everyone will know, and no one can come along and point to business leaders and comment adversely about their salaries while at the same time they are drawing down the same high salary or perhaps more.
On that, Mr. Speaker, I will now draw my remarks to a close.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on Bill C-18, a legislation to amend the Anti-Inflation Act. Inflation has become a real psychosis over the last ten

April 6, 1978
Anti-Inflation Act
years and remains a major barrier to the realization of our collective and individual aims.
In 1975, Mr. Speaker, when we were discussing Bill C-73 on price controls, I stated that the restraint measures the government intended to take did not strike at the roots of the problem. Indeed, controlling the salaries of the workers and the weak and letting the brass do as they wished was no solution and changed absolutely nothing to rising inflation. I would now add that the efforts that were being planned for the three following years would not solve the problem.
Mr. Speaker, today, after three years of implementing the Anti-Inflation Act, the government is out of breath in every field, and especially with regard to inflation and unemployment problems. It admits candidly that it is incapable of throttling rising prices and unemployment. When the price and wages control program was introduced, the board was given the task of reducing inflation to 6 per cent over a two-year period. Unfortunately, the system created a majority of dissatisfied people and much dissatisfaction and we are grappling with a 9.5 per cent inflation today. That is as unacceptable as the current rate of unemployment. Mr. Speaker, we not that the steps taken by the government until now, that is limiting government expenditures, controlling and watching prices as well as salaries, are precisely that, just steps. It is high time we have a cohesive policy, and over-all policy requiring decisive leadership. It is all too easy to blame inflation on unions and workers.
The inflation we know in Canada is not inflation created just for lack of demand as some would have us believe: it is monetary inflation stemming from the level of prices and interest rates. It is therefore a monetary problem. Let us not forget that the production of goods and the production of money, that is the issuing of credit, are the fruit of two entirely different processes. The price mechanism is related directly to the monetary system. Mr. Speaker, the chartered banks can issue up to 16 times the credit they have in real reserves; they have a direct influence on the purchasing power of consumers. High interest rates mean additional costs for the producers who pass them on in their prices. The consumer who resorts to credit to acquire goods and services will pay in the price of the products he buys a portion of the interest of the producer, in addition to his own interest on the capital.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, those who close their eyes on the impact of interest rates bury their heads in the sand, as the government is doing. The actions of the government relating to inflation controls were only reactions of defence. They came to grips with secondary effects rather than with the roots of the problem.
The government is unable to put before us a real aggressive policy to control inflation and unemployment. Does this mean that it has already surrendered to the financial power of chartered banks and large companies? We often hear in government circles that our inflation comes from external

causes and that it is worldwide. I would like to remind you that the most industrialized countries in Europe, such as Germany and Switzerland, have the lowest inflation rates. The continuous rise in the cost of energy and food we experience will only be amplified by the drop in the value of our dollar, because we import many of our products in large quantities.
In my view, the decline of the dollar is caused by the lack of confidence of financial circles and international bankers in our economy and by the total lack of leadership to ensure its recovery. Inflation which continues and will continue to plague us can be attributed to a large degree to past mistakes by the monetary and fiscal authorities. And, unfortunately, the longer inflation goes on the more complex become the factors creating it.
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the government when they refuse to end the controls abruptly. We need a decontrol process which will not bring back the staggering rise in prices, but let ine add that these decontrol measures as proposed by this government will still create a great deal of frustration because we cannot endlessly count on such simple measures to stop the decline in purchasing power. To get to the root of the evil, what will be needed is a consensus of the three main components of our economy, that is management, labour and the government. I believe it is already generally recognized that this is a step toward a more consistent policy which would not favour one group at the expense of the other. This action has had good results in Germany and other European countries. However, more than a consensus among the three groups, the government will have to seriously consider revamping the present monetary system, where most of the credit power rests with the chartered banks. We all recall that in 1976-77, interest rates offered on savings accounts decreased fairly substantially and that despite this trend financial and banking institutions continued to charge interest rates of 13'/2 per cent or more.
Mr. Speaker, we cannot stabilize our rate of inflation by relying on measures such as anti-inflation controls, which affect only some facets of the economy such as salary increases and other secondary problems, while the brass continue on their merry way. I therefore ask the government that, in submitting the first phases of its decontrol program, it also propose a genuine policy aimed at reversing inflation and unemployment, which, in my opinion, are causing more harm than the problem of national unity.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I hope to see the government exercise more control over chartered banks, especially, of course, over the Bank of Canada, which is the foremost money and credit institution, so that it adopts a credit policy in line with the harmonious development of the Canadian economy. Such a credit philosophy, if I can use those words, will, in my view, stabilize the purchasing power of consumers. I therefore implore the government to consider these suggestions very seriously.
April 6, 1978

Mr. Speaker, we in this party are going to oppose Bill C-18 because it continues the inequities of the Anti-Inflation Act and, instead of ending in April, it is really going to continue until January 1, 1979.
I want to start by looking at what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had to say in his New Year's interview with Mr. Bruce Phillips of CTV. He was asked by Mr. Phillips how he would defend his economic record. When Mr. Phillips mentioned 9.1 per cent inflation for the last 12 months-as of that date-the Prime Minister said it was unfair to look at the year-to-year change in the consumer price index without reference to the over-all trend of inflation during controls. He went on to say, and I quote from the transcript:
We are still making the assertion that by the end of the three-year control period the inflation rate will have been brought down from the almost 12 per cent it was, to 6 per cent.
Again quoting from the transcript, a few moments later the Prime Minister said:
... that on the over-all three-year average we're going to be on target.
The Prime Minister was wrong both in his view of recent Canadian economic history and in his forecast.
First, from the historical point of view, inflation was not almost 12 per cent when controls were announced in October, 1975, but 10.6 per cent.
The target was not 6 per cent but 4 per cent at the end of the three-year controls program. As for his forecast of getting 4 per cent this year, every economist I know of, in or out of government, forecasts that we will be looking to an inflation rate of 8 per cent for 1978. Given the recent increases in interest rates it is likely to average at least 8 per cent, and everybody knows that it is now about 9.5 per cent as measured by the consumer price index.
We all know that, on top of this, the unemployment rate this year will be at least 8 per cent, and if discouraged workers were counted accurately by Statistics Canada, there would be an average of 1-1/4 million workers unemployed, or 1,600,000 during 1978.
In several speeches I made when the Hon. John Turner was minister of finance-and our party has been consistent in this-I told the government that inflation cannot be controlled by deliberately creating more unemployment.
The current economic wisdom at the centre of the Liberal national economic policy was that expansionary policies would push up the cost of living, or the inflation rate. In our opinion, this is a fundamental error, with very bad results for the whole of this country but chiefly for low income areas of unstable employment. I think of Quebec and parts of Atlantic Canada such as my own, regions of northern New Brunswick, and most of Newfoundland.
The New Democratic Party was accused, both by Mr. Turner and Mr. Donald Macdonald, when each was minister
Anti-Inflation Act
of finance, of not caring about inflation. We retaliated by saying they were hurting individuals, regions, and national unity by their policy of waging the fight against inflation on the backs of the unemployed.
Just recently Mr. Ralph Sultan, chief economist of the Royal Bank of Canada, who is no wild eyed radical, said:
The current thinking is that expansionary policies would be inflationary. This may be one of our fundamental errors. Inflation seems built into our economy regardless of our growth rate.
The Prime Minister's economic policy for the last three or four years has been based upon this notion which is prepared to see unemployment rise as a trade-off for less inflation. Between 1975 and 1977 this policy was shown to be a bankrupt one, and 1978 will prove it to be even more so. Economic history attests that in Canada and other countries you cannot fight inflation on the backs of the unemployed and low income workers. It is not only a morally wrong policy but an economically bad one. That I repeat, has been shown in this country at the present time, and will be shown even more during 1978.
The Prime Minister pointed with pride in his recent address to the Economic Club of New York to the fact that Canada had created 280,000 new jobs between February, 1977, and February, 1978, "well above our historical average of 250,000 jobs each year." That is fair enough-if we do not seek the details of how many of these were permanent jobs. In any case, what he forgot to mention was that while jobs increased by 280,000 the demand for jobs rose by 362,000, leaving a record of 1,007,000 Canadians unemployed in February, 1978. Statistics Canada shows that there were only a little over 32,000 vacancies for permanent jobs in all of Canada during the same month. The Prime Minister conveniently did not mention that the size of the unemployed labour force in Canada had almost doubled since 1974, the year of the last election.
As high unemployment has continued there has been a substantial increase in the number of long term unemployed. The definition of long term unemployed that Statistics Canada uses is "unemployed for over 14 weeks". The number of people unemployed for 14 weeks and over averaged 247,000 in 1976, rising to an average of 302,000 in 1977.
In New York the Prime Minister tried to hide his government's miserable mismanagement of the economy since the last election by a curious selection of reference years such as 1964-when he was not Prime Minister-to 1975. He has done the same thing in the question period during this week. He does not dare run the coming election on his government's performance in the last four years, so he retreats to decade figures to try to hide from the Canadian people how poorly the Canadian economy has been managed over the last several years. This time, however, he will not fool the Canadian people.
The Prime Minister must have sounded unconvincing even to the Liberal faithful when they gathered in Ottawa in March, when he tried to tell them that Canada is a healthy country in a difficult world. Using unemployment as the chief yardstick of economic sickness, Canada has not fared well. The following are recent figures compiled by the International

Labour Organization in Geneva and the Montreal Gazette. These figures were published in the Montreal Gazette on Wednesday, February 8, 1978, on page 2. The countries with less than 4 per cent unemployment are: Switzerland under 1 per cent; Sweden 1.8 per cent; Japan 2 per cent; Austria 2 per cent; Norway 2 per cent; Israel 3.5 per cent; West Germany 4.2 per cent. Canada has in recent years one of the worst managed economies in the western world, and I could add the cost of living figures to go along with the unemployment statistics to show that. Amongst the western world countries, Canada has one of the most consistently high unemployment rates over the last three years. I would love to debate the Prime Minister's economic record during the coming election campaign, not the record of the government during the last ten years, but the record during the last four years since the last election campaign.
The Liberals are going to be fooled if they think that because of the Gallup polls which show them ahead because of the national unity issue, because the people in Quebec are uptight and so on, English speaking Canada will fall for that kind of thing and not see the economic mess that has been perpetrated by the stupid policies of this government in the last four years, and especially in the last three years.
Money policy or monetary policy was fairly tight in 1977 and was tightened even further by the Bank of Canada's two increases in its discount rate, which is the rate it charges to the banks that borrow from it, to 8.5 per cent from 6.7 per cent in March. These interest rate rises have occurred despite the fact that the Canadian economy is weak, a weakness that is widely attributed to the existence of deficient domestic demand for investment goods and consumer goods. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, imposing even higher interest rates on an economy already hampered by restrictive national and provincial fiscal policies will only serve to dampen business investment and consumer spending further. This again is another bleak chapter in the bankrupt economic policy which has been followed by this government.
For the first time since the Central bank adopted the policy in 1975 interest rates have been increased with no pretense that the change was needed to keep the supply of money growing within the chosen target range. In fact, the latest increase in the bank rate will probably make the money supply grow slower than the Bank of Canada says it needs to grow for the good of the economy. This means that interest rates are going higher than they should.

The rise in the bank rate immediately caused an increase in the prime rate charged by the ordinary banks, in other words, the interest rate which they charge to large corporations for short term loans. And with the prime rate up to 9.25 per cent, other interest rates will rise too. This can be expected to make it less attractive to build homes or to get business loans in order to improve one's business, or for consumers to buy durable goods such as automobiles, etc. Interest rates for loans such as these will be higher. The increases are far from over. They may be able to hold them in line until election time, but I doubt it because as I see it there are higher interest rates in the offing. These trends will all tend to hold the economy back at the very time when it needs to grow faster to cut down on unemployment. We are all familiar with the figure that it is over 1 million people. If you count the discouraged people who cannot get jobs and those who have given up looking for jobs and are therefore not counted statistically amongst the unemployed, the figure is at least 1.4 million people in Canada without jobs.
But Mr. Gerald Bouey, the governor of the Bank of Canada, admitted as he raised the interest rate, that the bank, and I quote him, "gives high priority in its conduct of monetary policy to the external value of the Canadian dollar." When is this government going to learn the lessons of the economic history of this country? It is repeating the same errors of the early 1960's.
Ottawa's actions of accommodating and encouraging higher interest rates in Canada at this time are explained on the basis that interest rate rises in Canada are inevitable because of interest rate pressures in the United States. Thus this government has chosen to defend the Canadian dollar at the cost of an even more sluggish economy. That means, in every day words, at the cost of more unemployment and at the cost of higher inflation. As Mr. Donner, a Toronto economist, said in the Globe and Mail yesterday "this risk is not worth taking, and Ottawa has, once again, chosen to emphasize the wrong priority. Ottawa has linked Canada's economic prestige to a particular international price for the Canadian dollar, and by intervening with tighter monetary measures in exacerbating the real No. 1 problem, which is not the declining dollar, but high unemployment."
As Clarence Barber, professor of economics at the University of Manitoba, has recently noted, the governor of the Bank of Canada claims to have a policy of gradually reducing the rate of inflation. "In fact, the evidence suggests that it has a policy of gradually increasing the rate of unemployment."
Since the governor embraced his monetarist creed-and for those who are not cognizant with the term "monetarist creed", it means the money supply aggregates are much more important than the interest rates and one does not intervene in the economy. The governor of the Bank of Canada embraced this very much since 1975. Now he has to get off that kick of Professor Milton Freidman and others. I repeat that the governor embraced his monetarist creed in the late summer of 1975, and Canada's unemployment has risen from 7 to 8.3 per cent. As Professor Barber says, and I am still quoting, "that
April 6, 1978

takes some doing when the U.S. economy is recovering and its unemployment rate is falling." Meanwhile, the new wage and price controls policy appears to have had little effect on the rate of inflation. That is a serious warning from Professor Barber.
The American economy is showing a decrease in unemployment and a decrease or a holding the line of inflation. When our economy should be moving up and our exports should be increasing, what do we get? We get increasing unemployment and higher interest rates that will further increase unemployment and the cost of living.
If we look two years ahead or more, this country will be in an even more serious condition than at the present time. I defy anyone to say that is gloom and doom. What we are going to get willy-nilly is the continuance of the policies of the past three years by this government which have made this country so badly off, both nationally and internationally, and have caused so much suffering to the people of this country.
This government's major thrust since October, 1975, when it introduced the anti-inflation legislation, has been to fight the cost of living or inflation, as measured by the consumer price index, by increasing unemployment. It is helping to convince many, as Karl Marx pointed out in the nineteenth century, that, in order to succeed, capitalism needs a "reserve army" of the unemployed. This time the major part of the army is young adults and housewives whose incomes for family well-being are desperately needed by at least half of Canadian families.
The record of this government for the past three or four years in its economic mismanagement of this country defies description. To continue essentially until January 1, 1979, with this present anti-inflation program which has not stopped price increases except in a marginal way, and in the past year especially has attacked the personal disposable income and wages of the ordinary people of this country, is a sad state of affairs, for a party to go to the nation with at such a time with such a program. They will try to hide behind the flag of national unity. This time those living in regions of high unemployment, and suffering desperately as a result of it, are not going to be fooled.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT AMENDMENT TO EXTEND RANGE OF PERSONS TO WHOM ANTI-INFLATION GUIDELINES APPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are now debating the demise of the government's anti-inflation program. Inflation has gone from 10.5 to 9.5 per cent, not much to show for almost three years. The Anti-Inflation Board will carry on for at least another 12 months.
I would like to speak today on a few of the elements in the inflationary process and the fact that other and more pressing problems are weighing down on us. With the Canadian dollar at a 45-year low, the American dollar collapsing on the world markets with its enormous American trade deficit, the Russian superiority in arms and their ability to control western oil through their successes in the Horn of Africa, along with Iraq and Libya, this means that Canada and the western world are in a rather grim financial situation. The value of oil has been a
Message from the Senate
factor in rising inflation. Inflation grew out of the oil crisis in 1973.
I would like to deal first with the Prime Minister's desire to have the Anti-Inflation Board grafted on to the Economic Council of Canada. There is a certain relationship in that one of the Council's jobs has been to give advice on how to avoid inflation. But the move does seem to pose great problems for the Economic Council if it is to have a function to point the way to the government of often unpleasant political truths. Will it not lose a great deal of value if it only becomes the mechanism for deflecting criticisms that rightly belong on the government's own shoulders?
One cannot quarrel with the idea of a general report and surveillance of inflationary processes. The problem will begin when the organization has to do what the Prime Minister suggests, and I quote:
-the surveillance of those particular cases of increase in prices, wages or other incomes which constitute threats to the national economic objective.
There does not seem to be any way in which the council can stay out of public controversy over its views on price and wage amendments. What is the government doing? It surely seems to be unloading on the Council the government's responsibility for the problems of inflation and it will almost certainly lose its role as an independent economic critic.
Obviously it is not going to develop new ties with organized labour or provincial governments. If the Economic Council is going to be involved in economic debate, there is substantial evidence that it would be better not to involve the Council. With such a move it will make the Council much less important in the future, and much more suspect to government direction. In the final analysis, the Council was set up to point the way in a non-political manner as the best advice for the government in dealing with economic problems.
Obviously the government's plan and the oft-stated hope that inflation would fall to 6 per cent by this year are purely a mythical mirage and a political deception. The announcement yesterday that the Bank of Canada's lending rate was up to 8.5 per cent, with two raises within the past month, indicate that the government is in serious difficulty. It was necessary to arrange an increase on its stand-by credit from $1.5 billion to $2.5 billion, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) announced that he had to draw $750 million to bolster Canada's foreign exchange reserves. Furthermore, the government lost $500 million through intervention in the foreign markets during March through interventions aimed at supporting the Canadian dollar, although the minister keeps saying that the Canadian dollar is floating. He said: Mr. Speaker, I want to thank hon. members of the House for giving unanimous consent to proceed today to the final stages of this bill. That unanimous consent is very much appreciated by me as the sponsor of the bill, and I know also by the seconder of the bill. We do appreciate this cooperation.
I would like to thank hon. members of the House for the consideration they have given the bill over the past 14 months. I would also like to express my appreciation for the expeditious work this morning of the members of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. That committee is heavily charged with other important legislation, and its members did undertake to facilitate the consideration of this bill and particularly the amendments to this bill this morning, so that once again there has been a very cooperative attitude in the House, which is very much appreciated.
April 6, 1978

Circulated amongst us is the amended version of Bill C-1001. It incorporates the changes made this morning in the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. I would like to refer very briefly to those changes. They can be found in a pledge made by me as sponsor of the bill in the debates of March 16 at pages 3846 and 3847 of Hansard. They, and they only, are the changes which were incorporated in this printed version this morning in the standing committee.
Those three changes are these: Former clause 2 has been amended in that former sections 5.2 and 5.3 have been entirely deleted from the new version of the bill. Former clause 4 which was found on page 8 of the bill has been entirely removed from the new bill. Finally, two words have been deleted from former clause 6 at line 6 of page 9. Those changes are in exact accord with the commitments made in my statement of March 16 which are recorded in Hansard at the pages to which I have referred, and which were made in the final stages of second reading debate. As I pointed out, no changes other than these have been made in the bill.
Just to remind the House again, the effect of the amendments are also as recorded in Hansard for March 16, and I will refer to them very briefly. The effect of the changes is to withdraw from the bill the request for a letters patent procedure for any possible future changes and the request for a negative resolution procedure in the House or in parliament as a future means of amending Bell Canada's basic charter.
Furthermore, the amendments would also withdraw the request formerly made for certain ancillary powers sought through the application to Bell Canada's charter of section 16 of the Canada Corporations Act.
Finally, through the deletion of the two words I mentioned the amendment would withdraw the request in this bill that future individual common stock issues not require CRTC approval. The effect of this latter change would be that future capital stock issues would require CRTC approval.
These are the important amendments made to this important private bill. What remains is an authorization of a new and higher level of capital for Bell Canada, and certain provisions to give Bell Canada a greater financial flexibility in capital stock. Those are the changes, and I believe they are such that the bill will now commend itself to hon. members of the House.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-1001, dealing with Bell Canada and as amended by the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, is acceptable to the New Democratic Party. Hon. members will recall that when this bill was first introduced in the Senate as Bill S-2, we objected to its passage in its original form because we felt that it would reduce parliamentary scrutiny of this monopoly telephone company. If the bill had passed unamended, it would have created a company which would have come
Bell Canada
under the Canada Corporations Act and therefore treated as any other corporation in Canada. Bell, by virtue of being a monopoly, should not be treated as any other corporation.
The bill would have allowed Bell Canada to expand and invest in non-telecommunication industries, which was prohibited by this parliament when it first granted Bell its act of incorporation. We felt that, if that was allowed, telephone subscribers would receive poorer service since their subscriber fees would be funneled off into non-related telecommunication undertakings by Bell Canada.
Another part of the bill to which we objected was the procedure of letters patent whereby Bell could change its act of incorporation to a negative resolution procedure, which in effect would have curtailed debate in the House on Bell's performance and the implications of any such changes. As well, we objected to removing CRTC scrutiny of the issuance of stock. Anyone who reads the debates of this Chamber will realize it was primarily the objection of the NDP that has brought about these amendments. We have had assistance from our friends in the Creditiste Party on occasion, and we appreciate that, but not one Liberal or Conservative member, other than the sponsor of the bill, rose in objection to these provisions in the bill which we say would have jeopardized telephone service and would have lessened parliament's scrutiny over this company.
Indeed, I think it is a sad chapter in the history of this parliament that the Minister of Communications (Mrs. Sauve) and her department, as well as the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, and CRTC, did not come forward with a public statement on what they thought the implications of the passage of this unamended bill would be on Bell Canada and its subscribers. Indeed, the length of this debate on Bill C-1001 almost reached the point of 1,001 speeches, because it was only through the NDP consistently putting up members during private members' hour every second Thursday that we were able to prolong debate on this bill and prevent its passage in original form until Bell Canada decided to make some compromises and withdraw the offending section of the bill. It took Bell a long time, in my opinion, to come to its senses, and indeed it is in the dying days of this parliament that it is finally getting in the bill its capitalization increase which still remains.
One of the issues on which we in this party have been harping again and again, not only before regulatory agencies but in this chamber, is the level of service that Bell is providing to its subscribers, which we say can be dramatically improved in terms of Bell's priorities, on where it is placing its priorities, and what it is doing with the rate increases it is receiving from the public. We have harped on the lack of improvement in the rural service over the years, and I think we have made an impression on Bell Canada officials that they have an obligation to rural subscribers to improve service so that we no longer have the norm of ten people per party line but have brought it down to more reasonable levels of four or

April 6, 1978
Bell Canada
two parties on a telephone line. As I say, we have made some progress in this respect.
I do not want to prolong this debate. I have spoken on this issue many times in the House, and anyone can look at the Hansard record to see the reasons why we objected to the bill. I think the bill is improved because of the amendments we have been able to win out of Bell Canada, and I hope that in the future when Bell Canada comes before the House to advocate changes in its act of incorporation, we, as members of parliament, will again have the opportunity to hold up to public scrutiny the activities and performance of Bell Canada, as is surely our right as members elected by constituents who are subscribers to this company.
Our whole aim during this debate is to maximize service to telephone subscribers, to pressure Bell Canada to live up to its responsibilities, and to keep Bell Canada involved in what its act of incorporation charges it to be involved with, that is, telephone service to the best of its ability for its subscribers at the most reasonable cost. We have won this battle here in the House of Commons. There is yet the battle before the regulatory agencies on rate increases which my colleagues and I will continue to fight in the interests of subscribers.

Mr. Speaker, I realize that I run the risk of being accused of just giving in public a bouquet I could give to my hon. friends in private, but I do not feel I should let this moment pass without paying a tribute to the tremendous piece of work that has been done on this legislation by the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes), the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), and other members of this caucus. I could say, of course, that it is a demonstration of what can be done by hard work in parliament.
I would also like to commend the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell) on his flexibility and his willingness to advocate that certain changes be made. At any rate, the story does have a happy ending although, as my friend has said, there are battles to be won in other places. But I did feel that I should not let this moment pass without paying this tribute to a number of my colleagues, and especially to my friend, the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie.

Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I think there was unanimous consent prior to this day that the next item, which is item No. 2, shall stand.
We will next proceed to Motion No. 50 in the name of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale).

That an order of the House do issue for a copy of the report by Hay Associates Ltd., management consultants, concerning the management of the Post Office Department, together with a list of the recommendations implemented by the department.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion first came up for consideration of the House on December 7 last. It is a very simple motion which should have received the approval of the government at that time.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the President of Privy Council (Mr. Pinard), rather than approving a motion of this kind, which was an attempt to get information to deal with the growing malaise in the Post Office Department, said that it is a confidential report. Perhaps I should quote him. He said:
These are internal working documents of a confidential nature. Consequently, I would ask the hon. member to withdraw his motion.
Then the motion was transferred for debate. I do not want to speak at length this afternoon because I hope that the matter will come to a vote.
Since great concern has been increasing in recent days regarding the problems of the Post Office, I would think hon. members would only be too happy to have access to information which would provide some answers in coming to grips with these problems. Certainly this opinion has been expressed almost every day in questions put from all sides of the House. Even the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) agrees that something has to be done.
There was a great celebration today, because of the significant anniversary of the Prime Minister becoming leader of the Liberal party ten years ago. During the question period it was demonstrated that the right hon. member has not been too accurate in some of his positions, statements, and actions over the intervening ten years. In 1973, when a government backbencher asked a question of the Prime Minister arising from the continuing long saga of the Post Office horror story, he answered briefly and succinctly by saying "Everybody knows postal service is lousy". He was dead accurate in his assessment of the situation. Obviously action must be taken. Before action can be taken, it must be based upon informed opinion.
The Hay report, which was produced at considerable expense to Canadian taxpayers, goes back to December of 1975. It was a report on major organizational problems in the Post Office Department. It was made up by departmental officials, in cooperation with members of the task force from the Treasury Board, which has a responsibility for administrative matters in the Post Office. It was compiled at great cost from a series of conferences, interviews, and consultations with members of the Post Office from all parts of the country. It is
April 6, 1978

an excellent, useful, and helpful document in coming to grips with these problems. Why should the government regard a public document of this kind as confidential? It is beyond my understanding. Surely the government must be interested in resolving the problems of the Post Office. That department will play a major role in the events which are not too far ahead. It is typical of an almost paranoid government to be concerned about confidentiality and secrecy. In fact, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) has been promoting successfully a piece of legislation on freedom of information. I trust the matter will come to vote today.
On the basis of the general concern which has been expressed for a long time, and which has grown in intensity in recent months as the problems become more critical, I hope we will receive the approval of hon. members for the tabling of this document, so that we will have access to its valuable information, and in turn begin to make recommendations for solving the Post Office problems. It is obvious to hon. members present in the chamber at this time that I have a document in my hand.
Table it.

I would be quite happy to. Whether it is the real document or a reasonable facsimile thereof, I do not know. It indicates the problem the government faces when it attempts to conceal information which has no confidentiality aspect whatsoever. The only legitimate reason I can conclude for this action is that there is information in the document which is embarrassing to the government. It is highly critical of the lack of attempts on the part of the government to deal with the growing problems of the Post Office.
The document recommends what hon. members on this side have been advocating for a long time, that is, the setting up of a special committee. We have not specified the specific terms of reference of the committee or its organizational structure. We have suggested that it could be a joint committee including members of the Senate and members of the House of Commons. Joint committees have been successful in coming to grips with problems on many occasions. It could be a special committee of the House assigned the task of pursuing a particular problem, as was the case regarding problems in the penitentiaries which the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs dealt with. It could be a subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications which deals with Post Office matters. It could be a royal commission as recommended by the Canadian Union of Postal Workers. Whatever its formation might be, it is encouraging to realize that the Hay study group made exactly the same proposal back in 1975.
I should like to quote from the report of the Joint Post Office-Treasury Board Secretariat Study Group, which reads as follows:
The study group, in beginning its assignment, excluded from its analysis any examination of organizational options for the Post Office such as a Crown corporation, special status department, etc., focusing instead on the internal structure of the existing department. The group took this particular course of action, not out of conviction that such options were impractical, but rather
Post Office
because it considered that manpower and time limitations made such a review infeasible and better studied later as a separate issue.
One of the first recommendations of this group, which was brought together in 1975 to investigate the Post Office and to come up with solutions, was that it had only gone partially into its investigation and that it must be followed up, if solutions were to be found, by another review at a later date to consider and study such important issues as the advisability of transforming the Post Office Department into a Crown corporation type of organization.
Now, I do not have to recite the problems of the Post office here today for it has been post office week in the House of Commons. We have had several debates on the subject which indicates the degree of concern with respect to post office problems. I do not have to repeat the problems. They are all too obvious.
I would like to comment on a statement that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) made recently when he said that there are far too many leaks from government departments. I do not know whether the document which I have in my hand is a leak or not. I cannot say because I have not seen the original document. He made some strong criticisms of public servants who might be responsible for such leaks. I suggest that in view of some of the problems in the body politic in Canada today

and the post office is typical of this type of situation-anybody with the courage of his convictions to make available to the general public, through elected representatives of the people, helpful documents of this kind is not acting in a despicable way. Rather, he would be acting in a responsible way, realizing that it is the only way that there can be any action obtained from a government that has been noted for inaction, wrong action, or just plain muddle-headedness.
I would say that the explanation of confidentiality is not in the interests of the public of Canada but in the interests of the government of Canada, the particular party in power. This is a far different situation from the one of confidential documents that border or move into the security area of concern.
It is another sad commentary on the lack of competence on the part of the present government that hon. members who have been primarily concerned with post office affairs and endeavouring to come to grips with the problem have had to go outside the country for information. We have not had a thorough study of the post office since 1966. I have that document in my hands, incidentally, and it is called the Royal Commission on Working Conditions in the Post Office Department, an excellent report under the chairmanship of the Hon. Andre Montpetit which was tabled in 1966, 12 years ago.
Strangely enough, it is in the intervening years that the Post Office Department has gone continuously downhill. There are 363 pages of recommendations, reforms, legislative changes and administrative changes that will have to be brought in urgently if the Post Office Department is going to meet the challenges of the revolution in communications generally that has been felt in Canada and throughout the industrial world. If

April 6, 1978
Post Office
I had time here this afternoon I could recite recommendation after recommendation to which no attention has been given by the government of Canada. The Liberal party has been in power during this whole period of time.
The latest document I received on the subject was put out by the Congress in Washington, where they have gone the route of the public corporation in order to deal with the problems of an industrial organization such as the modern post office. I refer to volume one of the report of the commission on the postal service, and it was brought down last spring. I refer to it at this time because it indicates that if we had access to this information from a Canadian source we could intelligently and hopefully sort out the post office confusion.
One of the topics they dealt with and which we have not started to deal with in Canada is the impact of electronic communications. There was a newspaper report recently that a firm in Toronto has launched itself into the electronic communications business in Canada. If the post office service was to go electronic, 70 per cent of the first class business would be removed. Seventy per cent of the post office business can be handled by electronic communications, and the technology is already available. Surely this subject requires careful examination.
Other topics in this report are financing the postal service- that is a topic that comes up repeatedly in this House-and levels of service. Hon. members know the horror stories we hear every day in question period in this House of Commons. Chapter six deals with postal rates and mail classification.
I understand the committee on statutory instruments has picked up this topic once again and they are standing by the decision they made with respect to irregular increases in postal rates by the government under administrative decree and order in council rather than by amending the Post Office Act as is required under the act. This is a fundamental invasion, as Senator Forsey keeps saying, of the rights of parliament because only parliament can increase taxes; but the government is increasing taxes by order in council.
The joint committee made up of Senators and members of the House of Commons only this morning was wrestling once again with this problem. They are concerned that the government has again ignored their unanimous recommendation, which states that order in council action is a fundamental violation of the rights or parliament. It is also a fundamental violation of the rights of parliament for the government to refuse the tabling of a report, a helpful, innocuous report so far as the security of Canada is concerned. Indeed, I think it would be helpful to the well-being and security of Canada if we did have access to this information and were able to make recommendations helpful in resolving post office problems.
I hope that hon. members will support this appeal this afternoon and vote positively so that the Hay report can be tabled. I think that we will all benefit from the information that is obtained. When it is observed in that report that the final recommendation was that it should be followed by another study, then we will have strong support for that viewpoint as well.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to indicate to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) that we are regularly and constantly receiving reports on the conditions which exist within the Post Office Department. If we seek and obtain these reports, it is because we want to study them, determine how we can implement the recommendations they make to improve the Post Office organization. For the information of the hon. member, I should like to say that I have with me a list of all the reports which have been prepared since 1969. There are several of them, and I do not understand why the hon. member has chosen to pay more attention to the Hay report than to the others.
The hon. member has mentioned a lack of attempts on the part of the government to come to grips with the problems within the Post Office. I suggest that if he would only read my communications, as well as the official report of our proceedings, he would find that we have indicated on several occasions the actions we have taken. As to his suggestion about a Crown corporation, a special commission of the House or a royal commission, I have said and I repeat that they all seem great to us, but before we decide on one of them and implement it, 1 feel we must find solutions to two problems. As I stated again recently, the Post Office is faced with two problems, namely the debugging of our mechanization and especially, our relations with our employees.
About the Hay report, perhaps I should say something. We have received several reports, including the Montpetit report, and I should like to indicate to my hon. colleague that we have implemented over 80 per cent of its 200-odd recommendations. Which proves that when we receive a report containing recommendations, we pay them the attention they deserve. We implement those which we feel are more likely to improve the postal service. That is what we have been doing and will continue to do. As to the Hay report-

The purpose of this study was to collect objective and realistic data from the various levels of management of Canada Post concerning their conception of the climate of the organization. In fact, the consultants, Hay Associates of Toronto, called the report a "Climate Analysis Report". That was in 1975, three years ago. The purpose of the report was to analyse the data and compare results with those from other employers. Hay Associates have also conducted a climate analysis report for the Royal Bank, Abitibi, Cominco and CMHC, to name a few.
Hay Associates aimed at ascertaining what were the strengths of the post office and what were the weaknesses. We are not hiding anything and I think we have a big problem. Any corporation with a budget of $1,300 million and around 63,000 employees has problems these days.


April 6, 1978

The hon. member opposite spoke of the United States post office. A report in the Washington Post of March 22 says there is talk of a postal strike in the United States. I can also send the hon. member a book published in the United States in the last year entitled "United States Post Office-A Great Mess". I think we all have problems in this world when we try to run large organizations.
Mr. Speaker, would the Postmaster General permit a question?

speechtext: Order, please.
The minister says the post office is in a mess now.
I am talking about the United States post office.
What about yours?

Ours is getting better and better every day. The survey attempted to show how wide the gap was between how things were in the post office and how they ought to be. It was a vast study. A total of 5,870 climate analysis questionnaires were distributed to various regions and to all levels of management. They were answered anonymously and returned directly to Hay Associates. The method insured that the managers were given every opportunity to be frank and candid.
The report's approach borrowed from contemporary sociology and reflects both the strengths and weaknesses of this method. That is to say, it aimed at determining what the opinions and attitudes of management were toward the organization that employed them. In no way did the report try to measure the performance, efficiency and rationale for organization and operational systems.
It must be emphasized that the report is essentially an aggregate of opinion and attitudes. While having some merit in learning what management thinks, the report's approach was essentially an academic approach to operational realities that remained constantly in flux as a result of the introduction of new techniques and operational methods at Canada Post. That is why they recommended a further study.
The report was conducted in 1975, only a relatively short time after the post office had been decentralized. Automation had also only been recently introduced. As a result, when the Hay inquiry was conducted the post office was still in a period of transition, a period of change. As celebrated English journalist, G. K. Chesterton, once said, "Progress is the maker of problems."
The post office, at the time of the Hay report, and indeed today, was and is changing, a change in many respects in the direction of progress. Traditional methods were being modified in the interests of progress, and as G. K. Chesterton stated, problems accompany a period of change.
The Hay report reflects the dismay and even at times the trauma experienced by some of the management at Canada
Post Office
Post. The old, safe routines were being uprooted and new ways of doing things remained to be modified and adjusted to make the new systems work smoothly.
This is not to say that management's attitudes as portrayed in the Hay report were entirely negative. Neither were they 100 per cent positive. To be frank, the Hay report did reveal that there existed some discontent at Canada Post about the way the organization was being run. There exist some problems and nobody is surprised about that. But the fact that senior management at Canada Post in 1975 wanted to ascertain what the sentiments of their management were vis-a-vis the organization is a tribute to their concern about improving the morale and productivity of their employees.
It would be grossly irresponsible for me here to reveal with any precision the details of the report. Certainly, the frank and candid opinions expressed in the survey could conceivably turn a branch against another branch, a division against a division, perhaps even a region against a region. Certainly, such a revelation would not be in the best interests of the Canadian public and Canada Post. Revealing the report's details would clearly serve no useful purpose except, perhaps, to reveal that there is some latitude for more changes at Canada Post if service is to be improved. And, let me ask, what organization made complex and sophisticated by having a staff of more than 60,000 scattered across several thousand miles does not have latitude for change and improvement?
I should also like, Mr. Speaker, to give a report about the status of our relations with our employees. There are five major unions in the post office.

There are five major unions in the Post Office Department. Following the Hay report, we have used several means and approaches to improve relations between employees and management. That is the kind of system we have put into place through inter-group sessions and consultation meetings with our employees. The management works exceptionally hard with four of our five unions. I need not remind my colleague from Brandon-Souris of the interventions the Canadian Union of Postal Workers have made during the convention of the Canadian Labour Congress in Quebec City, as reported in newspapers over the last four or five days. Hon. members will admit, if they really want to be fair, that we are dealing with people with whom it is quite hard to negotiate and to discuss and I suggest that the major problem in the Post Office is located at that level.
If all our labour unions co-operated with the Post Office, we could give you a service which would be as competitive and efficient as that of any other administration of the same type or size. At this point, concerning labour relations between the Post Office and its staff, I woud like to read to you an excerpt from a brief which was sent to me and which is entitled Labour Relations', it may be a very delicate subject, since the matter will probably be discussed soon or since we may have to take measures. My colleague says that we are not doing
