anything in the Post Office, that we are not trying to solve the problems. We are now in conciliation. The chairman has been appointed. In fact, he should begin conciliation talks next Monday. After a certain number of weeks or days of talks, or after both parties have made all their representations, he will prepare and table his report and then we will see what we have to do. If the union wishes to work more closely with us, we will try to solve the problem that way. I would like to quote a few comments on this subject:
If hon. members listen to their constituents and to the public these days who are indicating that the right to strike in the public service should be eliminated, it would be very easy to say yes right away. But the situation is more delicate than that. One has to understand the reason why the public voices such an opinion.
This opinion does not apply to all employees of the post office, but it is given because some workers of the union, at certain times act irresponsibly. Each work stoppage brings a rash of letters to editors suggesting that the right to strike be withdrawn or that the union be de-certified. All hon. members here have heard these cries. It is understandable the public eventually loses patience. As hon. members know, I sympathize with the Canadian public who get fed up at times with the kind of service that is given by the Post Office Department. I would like to point out that we are not the only ones responsible. We have workers who work well and we have certain workers who are not responsible in the work they do.
It is understandable as I say, that the public will eventually lose patience. It is questionable, however, that the answers suggested would solve the problems. According to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the right to strike is not the problem. In a letter to a major mailing organization the Prime Minister said that stifling the worst symptom of the ailment is not a cure. He suggests that we must deal with the perceptions that labour and management have of themselves as adversaries. The Prime Minister sees the basic challenge as one of securing from labour and management a sense of shared responsibility for making sure the enterprise survives. That is the basic point. If everybody in the post office were responsible about the work they had to perform, we would not have this problem, and we would not be in this mess, as it is called.
The Prime Minister points out that while cynics may scorn this approach in favour of a hard line, experience has proven that conflict between labour and management is neither inherent nor inevitable. Mr. Trudeau said-
Order.
You cannot say that, you must refer to the Prime Minister.
I am sorry, I will learn after a few weeks.
You are doing a good job, but you will only be here for a few months anyway.
Thank you, to the hon. member on the other side of the House, if that is the way to do it.
Yes.

The Prime Minister said "Consider the more harmonious relationships that exist in some other countries, for instance, West Germany. And in our post office, the letter carriers union is participating with management in a problem-solving program, which has succeeded in defusing some potentially explosive grievances." The LCUC have collaborated with us tremendously and we have no problem with them. The Prime Minister closed by insisting that his government will pursue its efforts to get all participants in collective bargaining in the public service to make the process work so that increased regulation does not become necessary.
Tripartitism is one of the many names given to an exercise in joint management/labour/govemment problem solving. This is an idea which is becoming more and more interesting to companies, labour unions and governments in their search for ways to cool the destructive aspects of confrontation and arrive at decisions which will present the optimum good to all three segments.
Tripartitism, it is hoped, will work for the welfare of the nation without the messiness of table banging, strikes, lockouts, and the impediment of passion. The conditions faced by most western nations-inflation, unemployment, slow growth, limited resources-enhance the appeal of any new ideas. Changes in the social climate, including interest in the quality of work, life, job enrichment, industrial democracy and individual social expectations, contribute as well to the search for new approaches to problem resolution.
It is clear that we must keep looking for better ways with an open mind. That is what we do. John F. Kennedy said, "Those who make peaceful revolution impossible make violent revolution inevitable".
Since the introduction of collective bargaining into the public service a number of bargaining agents have been certified by the Public Service Staff Relations Board to represent employees of the Post Office Department. The Canadian Union of Postal Workers represents approximately 25,000 employees primarily performing internal mail processing and complementary post services. The Canadian Union of Postal Workers was certified on January 16, 1975, at about the time of the Hay Report. The remaining 40,000 unionized employees are represented by the Letter Carriers' Union of Canada, the Association of Postal Officials of Canada, the Canadian Postmasters' and Assistants Association, the Public Service Alliance of Canada and the Professional Institute of the Public Service. These five unions present no problem.
What about the CLC?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I called it five o'clock I was speaking about the problems of the dollar. Roger Croft, a Toronto Star staff writer, under the headline "Moves to prop up the dollar called too little, too late", wrote the following today:
Ottawa's latest moves to prop the sagging dollar are too little, too late, most economists and foreign exchange dealers say.
... in hectic trading yesterday, the dollar skidded to yet another 35-year low at 87.4 cents U.S. before recovering slightly ...
But more important is the cost.
"We've got a run on the currency," Michael Graham, director of dealers A. E. Ames and Co. Ltd., told the Star.
"Foreign investors have lost confidence in the Canadian economy and are simply not putting their money into Canadian funds."
At the same time, added Graham, Canadians themselves are either buying real estate in Florida or opening up U.S. currency accounts "because no one in this country has any more confidence left.
"Both the Bank of Canada and the government have done too little, too late."
The article later refers to some of the reasons for our problems as follows:
"Our high inflation rate-after three years of wage and price controls-our high jobless rate, the big and growing budget deficits and the Quebec situation. Add the expected election to that lot, and no wonder everyone wants out of Canadian funds," Graham said.
Later in the article we find the following:
"No one wants to stick his neck out on that one" ...
This is a reference to where the Canadian dollar will go.
"We thought 95 was the psychological barrier late last year. Then it got to 90 and recently people have been saying that 87 cents will be the bottom."
There is now talk that at 85 cents there might be a turnaround. According to currency dealers, the Europeans got out of Canadian currency long ago. That is because they had sold off almost all they had. The article continues:
"The gnomes of Zurich have by now got out of the situation."
Barry Davenport, chief foreign exchange dealer with Wood Gundy Ltd. on Bay St. said he expects the dollar to continue "very, very weak for the foreseeable future."

April 6, 1978
Anti-Inflation Act
"It doesn't matter what the Bank of Canada or the finance minister do to stem the drop in the Canadian dollar. It won't have any effect. Things have to change..
Among those uncertainties, said Davenport, are the Quebec situation, the upcoming federal election and the relatively poor state of the Canadian economy.
Doug Peters, chief economist at the Toronto Dominion Bank, said ...
"The government should have convinced the speculators-whether corporate or private-that it meant business. I don't think the fundamental economic situation warrants this run on the dollar."
This is what Mr. Rogers, chief economist at the Bank of Nova Scotia, had to say:
There's talk and uncertainty about a new federal budget. But the sort of budget a government should bring in to deal with a run on its currency is a restrictive budget...
Finally, a senior partner at Dominion Securities Ltd. said that the only thing that can save the Canadian dollar is a new government. I think we can agree with that.
The Speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in New York about two weeks ago was really saying that "when you are broke you have to be kind to your bankers". In his speech he said that Quebec would not separate. Anyone who lends money would want to hear that. However, there are no assurances. It seems that our economic situation will not improve until the Quebec problem is settled. The flight of capital from that province, mainly to the United States, and the dislocating effect of language problems prevent the functioning of companies which must do business in other parts of Canada and in the United States. It is no wonder that business is moving out of that province. However, by attempting to shore up the economic life of Quebec the federal government is diverting large amounts of public funds into that province. Even with the most careful management it is difficult to allocate funds where they can have a meaningful and productive role.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and the Prime Minister have looked to the United States to bring the Canadian economy out of its doldrums. The United States is now obviously being geared to a much higher inflationary rate than was even considered a few months ago. There is no doubt that inflation in the United States is going up and is going to go up at a faster rate. The basic rate has moved from 6 per cent to 6V2 per cent and it will move to almost 7 per cent or more later this year. The United States coal contract will be a goal which other unions will strive to match, and they will prod non-union workers to demand increased wages. The United States dollar is weak, and ours is weaker. That will cause import prices to rise.
The President of the United States has had to back higher farm prices, stockpile copper and make a good many other promises in order to nail down votes to ratify the Panama Canal Treaty. On the political scene, the Panama Canal Treaty has increased the inflationary risk. The government and Congress are not likely to do very much about it. Mr. Carter will obviously look for other ways to deal with inflation, but he is not going to balance the budget. He wants tax cuts, and he will not restrain the money supply. Will the President

of the United States turn to what the AIB was supposed to do in Canada?
How will President Carter control wages and prices? He will obviously be forced into the same tactics used by the AIB. One tactic was to get at wages and prices directly. High wages and high prices are symptoms of inflation, not the cause. President Carter and other people around him know that controls have not worked in the United States, in Canada or in any other major country, so it is almost certain that United States inflation will race along and gather steam as the year goes by.
A previous minister of finance, Mr. Turner, always maintained that inflation arose outside the country and that there was nothing we could do about it. Inflation has created a voracious monster, and it may in time destroy our institutions. We have had a decade of accelerated inflation, and all indications are that we will have more in the next few years. We measure goods and services in terms of money prices. If we had a pure barter economy, there would not be generalized inflation. If the supply of money rises faster than the supply of goods and services, then prices for all goods and services rise as well. Only if the money supply does not become more plentiful relative to goods and services will inflation be contained.
In the early stages of inflation the total money supply declines as the public is duped into holding money at high rates of interest, but actually at negative real rates of return. As inflation advances the public tries to dump its money into buying goods before inflation reduces their value. But obviously credit must be settled at some time, and there is a limit to credit.
There are other inflationary factors which are new. Mr. Henry Kaufman, in an address to the Committee on the Budget of the U.S. House of Representatives, had this to say:
The composition of credit demands in 1978 reveals part of the emerging problem. I shall focus on three major demanders for money-the households, business and the Federal Government. The increases in consumer credit and mortgage debt, reflecting mainly borrowings by individuals, is truly spectacular.
This is referring to the American scene.
It reflects strong demands for consumer goods and housing, sharp increases in prices, and a new inflationary psychology that is perhaps more than marginally liberalizing the Financing attitudes and habits of individuals.
Our inability to reduce inflation is encouraging individuals to bid far more aggressively for mortgage funds than in the past because home ownership, at least in the postwar period, has been a far more satisfactory hedge against inflation than investments in financial assets ranging from savings deposits to bonds and to common stock.
So home ownership and various other personal needs requiring credit have certainly increased the number of problems related to borrowing. People's personal monetary habits spread over the nation as a whole, and that is important.
One of the greatest difficulties in steadying inflation is the definition of money. The Bank of Canada has standardized four types of money, and if the effect of money on inflation in real economic activity is viewed solely in terms of actual spending on goods and services, then we must look at spendable money. But when money is viewed as a commodity it seems to be a much broader concept. Obviously there should be a wider definition of money or of what should be called the
April 6, 1978

total money supply. If there is an excessive creation of money, it will undermine its value; if there is slow growth, it will raise the value of money.
It is obvious in an open economy such as is Canada's that large increases in money supply are not necessarily reflected in domestic price levels in the immediate future. In our open economy, an increase in the money supply so that the total supply of goods and services is greater than the productive capacity of the domestic market can be met by increased imports, because when domestic prices rise above competitive world prices an inflow of goods and services results. Obviously excessive money supply results in a severe deterioration in the current account of the balance of payments, with the consequent downward movement of the external value of the currency.
Canada has shown all the symptoms of excessive money creation in the early 1970's. The current account deficit was $4.8 billion in 1975; $4.2 billion in 1976; and $4.1 billion in 1977. How should one deal with the current account deficit? There are a number of ways of dealing with it, or one can use a combination of them all. Raising domestic interest rates, which the Bank of Canada has just instituted, is obviously one action which causes an inflow of money. But when we are hampered by political uncertainty in the country, with an election in the wind and with the problems with Quebec, this might offset the deficit, and tight money will eliminate the excessive current account. Also, the Central Bank could allow its foreign exchange reserves to run down, which would eventually diminish the money supply, or it could induce sellers to accept the local currency. Unless excessive monetary creation is stopped, money will either depreciate against local goods and services or against foreign currency.
Toward the end of 1976 the Bank of Canada allowed interest rates to fall and differentials vis-a-vis the U.S. money market to narrow sharply so that the excessive money creation in a little over a year has reduced the external value of the Canadian dollar by 13 per cent.
From 1967 to 1977 the growth of the money supply was truly phenomenal but the Canadian public was willing to hold increasing amounts of the total money supply as a percentage of its transactions. This was borne out in the annual report of 1976 of the Bank of Canada, which stated the following:
-the inference is that as incomes have risen over this period, most people wish to hold a larger proportion of their incomes in the form of interest earning deposits. In terms of our earlier discussions of velocity, it is also a way of saying that every dollar of money turned over fewer and fewer times in the past ten years to accomplish a given rate of economic growth. Excessive credit demands were being accommodated rather easily by the further creation of money, and therefore, interest rates were not allowed to perform their credit allocative function.
During the period of 1967 to 1977 three quarters of the increasing assets of the Bank of Canada have been ascribed to the purchase of Government of Canada bonds. Obviously the Bank of Canada has been monetizing government of Canada
Anti-Inflation Act
bonds, the result of which has been a rapid increase in inflation.
Supporters of Keynes point out the economic benefits of a budget deficit. They indicate that the Bank of Canada has had to increase its support as a percentage of the net financing requirements. In the last ten years the government of Canada has been unable or unwilling to obtain non-inflationary financing, such as sales to the non-banking general public, and has relied increasingly on the printing presses. Obviously credit demands rise faster than the money supply, with the competition for funds causing interest rates to rise, thus eliminating the weaker borrower, and if at this stage the central Bank keeps interest rates from rising too fast, it is forced to monetize the increasing credit amounts.
This happened in 1972 to 1974 with a minority government which feared that bad publicity would result. The result was that the Bank of Canada took up 6 per cent of the government's net financing requirements. According to the "Bank of Canada Review", in 1966 to 1968 the Bank of Canada purchased 18 per cent of the bonds, which amounted to $2,578 million. In 1972 to 1974 the Bank of Canada purchased 66 per cent of the bonds which amounted to $3,271 million. In the first nine months of this year, almost 23.5 per cent of the bonds was taken up.
It is obvious that the purchase of these bonds by the Bank of Canada has increased our rate of inflation. This enormous appetite of the public sector has crowded out the private sector, and the Bank of Canada rescued the Canadian government by purchasing much of its debt. The situation was turned back once more in the last year, and with the government's recurring record of a high budgetary deficit it is obvious that this year some 25 per cent or more will have to be monetized by the government and by the central Bank, thus increasing our financial and inflationary expectations.
In the fiscal year of 1978-79 the prospects are frightening. With a $10 billion deficit and, it is to be hoped, a reviving private sector, interest rates will be forced up to high levels or, what is even worse, monetization on a large scale will be required or the printing of more money. It is estimated that if the government monetizes only 25 per cent of its requirements in two years, we will have created $34 billion in total money, or an increase of 40 per cent in two years.
How inflation can be kept below double digit rates is not at all clear. A sensible approach for the government of Canada to take is to eliminate its $10 billion to $11 billion deficit which would allow the central Bank to follow non-inflationary policies. To raise taxes now would harm the private sector. To cut expenditures seems to be the best course to follow. However, the government has obviously decided to raise a substantial portion of its next financing abroad. The Minister of Finance should tell us what are his financing plans for the next year.
The floating of the $750 million loan is just the beginning, and the speech of the Prime Minister paves the way for the future. But how can he be so hopeful about the political realities in Quebec? Obviously the government hopes to borrow abroad so as to shore up the Canadian dollar. If

April 6, 1978
Anti-Inflation Act
foreign currency is exchanged for the Canadian dollar in a freely floating market, the net effect would be to raise the value of the Canadian dollar, with beneficial side effects on the anti-inflation effort. But if the foreign currency is converted into Canadian dollars and is absorbed into foreign currency reserves, the inflationary impact will remain the same. It seems that we will not have a balanced budget, and there are those who suggest that with the frightening prospect of two $10 billion to $11 billion deficits back to back, our rates of inflation could be double digit.
The demise of the AIB has to come. It was faulty in the beginning and it failed to attack the causes of inflation. All it dealt with was the symptoms, the rise in wages and prices. Inflationary forces were at work internally and externally and the government has done little about them.

The House resumed, from Monday, March 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. Whelan that Bill C-29, to amend the Farm Credit Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to indicate our party's support for the bill before the House tonight, in a mood of friendliness and co-operativeness, in order to expedite the work of parliament, and I will be as brief as I possibly can. The bill before the House tonight does a couple of things. It increases the Farm Credit Corporation's capital from $100 million to $150 million; it also increases the amount that can be lent to individual farmers under the Farm Credit Corporation. It increases the lending limits to $200,000 for all borrowers. At present the limitations are $150,000 for persons under the age of 35 and $100,000 for the people over the age of 35.
As I have said, the bill before us is a good bill; it will help farmers a little bit better in a pinch. But I want to make it clear that it will not solve their problems.
It will be worth while to take a few minutes to put on the record some of the statistics that show the reality of the problems faced by Canadian farmers today. I know of many members, even some from New Brunswick, who are not aware of the dire financial circumstances that farmers are faced with today in Canada. The number of farms in this country is decreasing every year. According to the census, from 1951 to 1976 the number of small farms in the small farm category,

April 6, 1978

which comprises acreage ranging from 70 to 759 acres, went down by 36 per cent. The number of farms in the 760 acre and more category went up by 72 per cent. One can see, Mr. Speaker, that farms in Canada are becoming larger and larger and more and more of the smaller farmers are being forced off the land.
Farm debt should concern all of us. We are discussing a bill to lend farmers money and farm debt is going up very rapidly. It is probably even going up in Crowfoot. For example, in 1966 we find that the farm debt in this country was some $3.4 billion; in 1976 the farm debt had gone up to some $9.5 billion. Farm debt is triple what it was previously.
Then if you look at net farm income, Mr. Speaker, one would assume that if the farm debt is going up, with people borrowing money and expanding their assets, then net farm income should likewise go up. We all know that farmers are hard working people. It should be pointed out to the people of Canada that the Canadian farmer is the most productive farmer in the world. It costs only about 14 per cent of our consumer dollar to buy food in this country, whereas in the United States it costs about 15 per cent of the consumer dollar. In every other country in the world costs are much higher than that. The Saskatchewan Wheat Pool recently used as an example a typical food basket and it was found that for that food basket in Canada it took about five hours and 15 minutes worth of labour to buy it. In Washington, in the U.S., it took about seven hours of labour to buy that same basket of food. In Toyko it takes around 24 hours worth of labour, and in Buenos Aires, Brazil, it takes approximately 60 hours of labour to buy the same basket of food. Once again we can see the Canadian farmer is indeed most productive. Canadian consumers are very fortunate that our farming system is efficient and we are able to produce food at a lower price than any other country in the world.
I suspect in some areas where food prices are high that it is not the fault of the farmer, it is the fault of the middleman. Again there are examples to point that out. For instance, using the consumer price index in January we found that the price of beef had gone up some 33 per cent. For a 1,000 pound steer we found that the farmer had received an extra 19 per cent in January, 1978, or an extra $80 over what he would have received in January, 1977. The consumer had paid an extra 33 per cent for the steer, or an extra $180. This meant the middleman had received an extra $100 for the steer for that same period. We looked at the statistics for these middlemen. We looked at wage rates first of all, because in this House there are hon. members who will say that the workers are making too much money. We found that the wage agreements for the packing house workers had increased only 6 per cent during that calendar year. So it was not the workers who were receiving that money.
One would assume with all this extra investment and the efficiency of the farmer, together with the free enterprise values in this country, that the farmer would be receiving a much higher income due to his initiative, hard work and all the
Farm Credit Corporation
expansion of his capital, his assets and the like. But that is not the case at all.
I have here before me the figures on net income for Canadian farmers. In 1974 net income was some $3.9 billion. In 1975 it had gone up to some $4.3 billion. In 1976 it had gone down to some $3.7 billion, and in 1977, according to the best estimates of Statistics Canada, it will be about $3.3 billion.
This means the farmers of this country had a drop in wages and salaries of some 23 per cent. Which other group in society would allow their wages to go down by that amount? That is what happened to the farmers of this country. It is net income they are losing, not their cash receipts.
At the same time as income went down, what happened to their costs? In 1975, farm costs in this country were $6.6 billion. In 1976 they were $7.3 billion and in 1977 it looks as though they will be $7.8 billion. Therefore, while the cost to the farmer increased by some 18 per cent, his net income dropped by 23 per cent. The Canadian farmer is expected to meet his 1978 costs with his 1974 income. That is not fair. Farm incomes must be higher. The farmer must receive a guaranteed price for his commodity. He must get a better break from the marketplace. The farmer is not receiving a break from this government.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has gotten up time and again in the House to say that we have the greatest farm programs and the wealthiest farmers in the world. I wish he would look at some of his own statistics which show that farm income has decreased drastically. Debts are piling up and farmers are being forced to leave the land.
Fet us look at more statistics which point out what is happening in rural Canada, particularly in my province. Yesterday I was astounded to find in some research we were doing that cash receipts in Saskatchewan for January 1978 had fallen by 55 per cent over January 1975. If the people in the constituency of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) had a drop in income of 55 per cent, she would scream blue murder in the House like I am trying to do now. That is the drop in cash receipts for Saskatchewan farmers between 1975 and 1978, according to the Department of Agriculture and Statistics Canada.
Fet us look at the Saskatchewan operating costs and depreciation charges. In the full year 1977, compared with 1975, the operating costs in Saskatchewan increased by 23 per cent. While cash receipts are down by 55 per cent, their costs are up by 33 per cent. Is it any wonder why grain farmers in my province, Manitoba and Alberta are going out of business? Is it any wonder more and more farmers are being forced to sell their land? The older farmers are selling to the big guy. Farms are consolidating very quickly.
Fook at net income in Saskatchewan. If you take away the cash receipts and leave in the farmer's pocket the money he is able to spend, you find that net income in Saskatchewan between 1975 and 1977 decreased by some 40 per cent.

April 6, 1978
Farm Credit Corporation
Stabilization programs will not rectify that situation in any serious way.
The 1978 forecasts for Saskatchewan indicate that costs will probably be 32 per cent higher than 1975 costs. The 1978 costs will be 105 per cent higher than the 1970 to 1974 average. In every province in this country there was a similar situation. I am sure the hon. member from British Columbia who will be speaking after me will be saying some of the same things about farm income.
Let us look at Alberta, the province of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) who is worried about his re-election in Crowfoot. In 1978, cash receipts in that province were down by some 38 per cent over January 1975. In Manitoba, cash receipts in January 1978 were down by some 53 per cent over 1975. In other words, the drop in Manitoba was roughly the same as the 55 per cent drop in Saskatchewan.
I have intentionally used a lot of figures and statistics to point out to the House and the government that there has been a serious drop in farm income. Passing a bill like this, even though it is good and will help some farmers in a pinch, is not good enough. We must start determining what we are going to do to ensure that farmers survive and that their family farm remains the basic unit of production. If we do not do that, the family farms will disappear. We will have a situation similar to that in states in the United States such as Colorado, where 95 per cent of the farmland is owned by non-farmers such as doctors, lawyers, wealthy people in the cities, corporations, real estate people and the like. The rest is owned by the farmers who are doing the farming. If we go that way in this country, it will not only be a disaster socially but economically, not just for the farmers but for the country.
As the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) has stated, we in Canada have a real crisis in unemployment. If we do not produce and process our food in Canada, we will add to that unemployment problem. In almost any food category in which we are not self-sufficient, we are not only losing jobs but a lot of money. We are only self-sufficient in a few items of food in this country. According to all indications, if we do not start changing our policies, by the year 2000 Canada will not be feeding itself. According to the Science Council, we will only be self-sufficient in five of the 27 basic foods in Canada.
According to the figures of the Minister of Agriculture, if we take away grain and oilseeds we will be in a deficit position in production of food to the tune of about $1.8 billion. That is a downright shame. Those policies have to change. One change should be to ensure that our farmers receive a decent wage. If they get a decent wage, they will produce food.
This country has the capacity to feed ourselves for hundreds of years in the future as well as the capacity to feed a lot of others in the world. We should be making a commitment to self-sufficiency. That would not only be good for rural Canada but for the urban consumer as well.
I want to use one example, that of broilers. There is now a move in Canada that is almost completed which I support

totally. That is the bringing in of a national marketing board to handle broilers and chickens across this country. We will have that marketing board as soon as the province of Alberta gives us the green light. The other provinces are pretty well in agreement.
In anticipation of a national marketing board, a number of large chicken importers in Canada have been importing an unduly large number of imports from the United States. They do that because, when a supply management board is brought in, import quotas will be based on the previous five year average. Therefore, they are importing five, ten, 15 or 20 times as many broilers as in the past in order to up their average of imports. In that way they will not be as controlled by the farmers' agency as they might otherwise be, as it is in terms of industrial milk, eggs and other products marketed through the marketing board in this country or through the provinces.
Studies have pointed out that in the last year in the area of chickens alone, literally tens of millions of dollars have been lost in productivity as well as jobs we would have had if we had not imported so many chickens from abroad. We should have been producing Canadian chickens, making sure that Canadian chicken farmers had better incomes and that Canadian workers eviscerated, processed and cleaned those chickens instead of letting that be done in the United States. We should have been making sure that Canadians in the transportation and refrigeration industries were given jobs transporting those chickens.
We have lost literally tens of thousands of dollars in that industry alone, but I could go through the whole food industry. I admit that I do not know very much about particular industries in Ontario, but I know that fruit and vegetable growers at about the time of the second world war supplied about 70 per cent of the Canadian market. I believe we now supply about only 30 per cent of our market. We have the capacity to be almost self-sufficient in fruits and vegetables, yet we are not. Because we are not, we are losing hundreds of millions of dollars which could be generated in Canada.
Our target must be to be self-sufficient in food. One way of doing that would be to make sure that farmers are guaranteed decent prices for their products. If they are guaranteed decent prices, they will produce food. Farmers are about the only people in our country who do not have guaranteed prices for their labour or their commodities, and they have to have guaranteed prices if they are to produce food. We have to produce food if we are to keep farmers on the farm and if we are to keep the rural fabric of our country going as strongly as it should.
I want to remind hon. members of these things because I feel that most Canadians think we can produce an infinite amount of food and that we are the bread basket of the world. People do not realize that with our existing policies, according to the government, the Science Council of Canada and almost every organization which has looked into this, by the year 2000 we will be a net importer of food. We will not be able to feed
April 6, 1978

ourselves, and that will be mainly because of policies which do not assist farmers to produce the food that they can be producing.
With regard to self-sufficiency, according to the federal government there are several hundred acres of good quality farmland being taken out of production each and every day. Because of our climate we cannot produce food in most of the country. We have lakes, water, muskegs, forests and places where food just cannot be produced. Only about 4 per cent of our country can produce food in great quantities, yet several hundred acres of farmland are being paved under each and every day or sold to developers for urban development and turned into such a state where the land cannot be recaptured for the production of food. I think that is a crime, and it should not go on. We should be concerned about producing as much food as we can in order to feed the people of this country, to stimulate our economy and to make our contribution abroad in terms of foreign aid.
I call upon this House to pass this bill as quickly as possible so that farmers who need more credit from the Farm Credit Corporation can get it. However, I ask hon. members on both sides of the House to realize that farming is important, that without the support of this government and governments right across the country there will be fewer and fewer farmers, and that the day will come when there will be a food shortage and we will be a net importer of food.
That might not sound very serious to many people, but there was a time when we did not worry about the shortage of oil. We said we could get all the oil we needed from the Arabs or Venezuelans at very low prices. That is the kind of policy we pursued for years, and now we have an energy crisis and a price crisis. If we do not have foresight, the same thing will happen with regard to food about 25 or 30 years from now. I ask hon. members, please, to do something about this now instead of burdening our children and our grandchildren.

speakeroldname: Hon. Daniel J. MacDonald (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I speak this evening on behalf of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan).
The Farm Credit Corporation has been administering the Farm Credit Act for close to 20 years. In that time, it has approved over 192,000 loans totalling more than $3.1 billion. A further indication of the importance of this agency is that it extends approximately 60 per cent to 70 per cent of all the long-term farm credit in Canada. In recent years, private lenders, the chartered banks in particular, have become more active in the general field of farm credit, and, more particularly, in the area of long-term credit. I sincerely welcome this increased participation. The Farm Credit Corporation is a long way from meeting the total demand, and unless steps are taken to meet it, the gap will continue to widen. Projections are that it will soon take close to $1 billion per year to meet the long-term credit needs of Canadian farmers.
This bill brings forth a number of amendments designed to update the Farm Credit Act so that Canadian farmers can
Farm Credit Corporation
maintain their position of leadership in the world and increase their productivity level through the wise use of credit.
The major amendments are as follows: the FCC's capital will be increased from $100 million to $150 million, thus increasing the corporation's borrowing capacity to $3.75 billion from $2.5 billion. There is real urgency for this amendment because the corporation's capital will be used up by May, 1978.
Most age restrictions on lending will be removed except for loans to persons phasing into farming. This special advantage would continue to be offered to persons under 35 years of age.
The maximum loan for a single farming enterprise will be increased to $200,000 for one qualifying applicant and $400,000 for two or more qualifying applicants.
Before going on to the lesser amendments, let me give the reasons for these three proposals. The present authorized capital of $100 million and the corporation's borrowing capacity of 25 times that, or $2.5 billion, will be exhausted early in 1978-79.
The corporation's capital was last increased in 1975 by about 50 per cent, from $66 million. Between 1971 and 1976 the total value of farm capital in Canada increased from $23.7 billion to $57 billion, representing an increase of close to 140 per cent. The number of farms with annual sales of $5,000 or more has increased by 18 per cent. The number whose sales exceed $10,000 increased by more than 63 per cent. The corporation therefore needs a significant increase in borrowing power to be able to keep pace with the increase in total farm capital.
In order to meet future demands we are also proposing that henceforth requests for additional capital could also be authorized under an appropriation act. Any provision of an appropriation act authorizing an increase in the aggregate amount would stand permanently referred to any committee of the House of Commons established for the purpose of reviewing matters relating to agriculture.
It should be noted that the FCC will continue to be restrictive in its lending guidelines in order to stay in line with the government's restraint program. This means that applications will continue to be assessed according to the applicant's need for funds from the Farm Credit Corporation.
The second amendment removes age as a qualifying factor for lending limits. Hon. members will recall that when the Minister of Agriculture proposed the 1975 amendments to the Farm Credit Act, the main thrust of that bill was to help young people get started in farming. Since then the FCC's total lending to young farmers has steadily increased. This year almost three quarters of all loans went to persons under 35 years of age. This represents some $410 million.
A great number of farmers, farm organizations and the FCC advisory committee as well as members of parliament have written to the Minister of Agriculture and made recommendations in the past few years. One of the points that constantly comes up is that need does not magically stop at 35.

April 6, 1978
Farm Credit Corporation
The present amendments extend these advantages to all farmers. Nothing is taken away from young farmers by these amendments. They simply acknowledge that basic credit requirements do not change on a specific birth date. Experience indicates that the imposition of the 35-year age limit encourages borrowers to rearrange business structures to qualify a spouse or child. This amendment will give more flexibility in meeting real credit needs. The 35-year age limit would remain on what we now call Part IV, or beginning farmer loans, which allow the borrower to retain an off-farm job for up to five years before becoming principally engaged in farming.
We must recognize that capitalization under all its forms is increasing in agriculture. With the farm labour problems of the past and the future, increased mechanization will continue. Many of the costs of technological change cannot be paid for immediately out of current incomes. Time is required. I wish to remind the House that in recent years the farmer has very often been faced with the cost-price squeeze. This cost-price squeeze has forced him to pay for most capital requirements over a substantial period of time.
The third amendment, therefore, deals with increases in lending limits. Under its present legislation, the Farm Credit Corporation can lend up to $100,000 for standard farm loans and up to $150,000 for loans for young farmers. The $150,000 limit for young farmers was set in 1975 and the $100,000 limit for the standard loans was set in 1972. According to Statistics Canada, land values have increased 25 per cent since 1975 and 130 per cent since 1972. Furthermore, a farm today is nearly 10 per cent larger than it was in 1975.
The present loan limit applies to farm units as well as to applicants. Thus, the maximum loan for a farm operated by father and child or by partners is presently $100,000 or $150,000, depending on age. If this bill is approved, the Farm Credit Act would provide a new loan limit of $200,000 per qualifying operator up to a maximum of $400,000 for a farm unit where there are two or more qualifying operators. We feel this will facilitate joint operations, encourage greater efficiency and a smoother phasing in of the young operator into the family farm business.
This increase in lending limits is presently necessary so that the Farm Credit Corporation can meet the credit needs of Canadian farmers. There are a number of sectors which have become increasingly difficult to finance. For example, a grain-livestock operation of some 1,100 acres in Alberta presently costs about $400,000. In Saskatchewan, let us say on the Regina plains, if one wishes to purchase two sections of wheat land it would likely cost over $500,000. In Ontario, a 75-cow dairy farm would cost more than $300,000. Cash cropping land of about 200 acres in size in southwestern Ontario would probably cost nearly $300,000 today. These are but a few examples of some typical capitalization requirements on family farms in Canada.

In looking at these proposed amendments, some critics will say that raising loan limits, removing the age limits and adding capital for the corporation will have an inflationary effect on land values. There may be a small element of truth to this statement since the provision of more adequate credit will at all times favour the buying and selling of land. However, farm land gets its value because of its capacity to produce income. It is really economic conditions-that is, the level of income produced-which are the main determinant of land prices, not credit. An increase in the lending limits and removal of age limits only mean that the farmer with the greatest need can more easily compete for the land available.
A small number of other amendments are included in this bill which are designed to streamline the administrative operations of the act. These are, first, the use of market value to assess all loans. The Farm Credit Corporation at present uses two values in assessing the security it takes: market value and appraised value. Generally, market values are used for young borrowers and the appraised value for older borrowers. Market value is based on recent sales of similar properties while appraised or productive value is mainly based on the capitalized value of net income. Appraised value is calculated, and therefore a theoretical value which is bound to confuse most people, other than economists. The use of these different values has been confusing to borrowers and to other agencies, as well as to FCC staff. In recommending the use of market value and repayment ability, it is understood that loan limits would be based on the lower of the two. This point should be stressed. No matter how high or low the market value, all loans are determined on the repayment ability of the proposed operation.
A second amendment regards the removal of the supervision fee. Under the original act passed in 1969, a supervision fee of $25 was set for supervised loans; that is, those that exceed 75 per cent of the appraised value. The fee is now more of a nuisance than anything else, and sometimes gets in the way of establishing good relationships between the borrower and staff. Under the proposed legislation, advisory services would be provided only where needed and wanted.
Third, there is the provision for losses on loans. The present act has established a reserve where actual losses have been charged. This amendment would allow the corporation to make provisions for these losses according to accepted accounting principles.
The last amendment proposes that penalty interest be dropped. It is believed that removal of penalty interest would make the Farm Credit Act more compatible with the spirit of the Interest Act, which prohibits penalty interest except in those acts which specifically provide for it. Even a higher penalty interest would probably not have the desired deterrent effect because farmers traditionally pay off loans as fast as they can, even when the interest rate is well below the market rate.
In 1978, farmers will face further increases in costs of farm inputs and the present outlook is for slightly decreased realized net income. When hon. members consider that these farmers
April 6, 1978

represent a mere 6 per cent of our population, yet they produce most of the food that all 24 million Canadians consume, as well as earn about $4 billion in foreign exchange from exports, they can understand the importance of these amendments. One of the tools of our modern economy, credit, must be available to the Canadian provider of food.
I also want to mention that loans under the Farm Credit Act are not a grant or a gift. Borrowers enjoy a slightly lower than market rate. The FCC interest rate is presently 91A per cent. On a $200,000 loan amortized over 29 years, this represents an average of $13,000 in interest payments alone per year. The Farm Credit Act is a tool which gives operators of family farms a chance to make a success of their operations. One need only look at FCC's statistics to realize that this opportunity is not taken lightly. Farmers have by far the best repayment record in our Canadian society.
I have faith in the ability of Canadian farmers to continue to produce high quality food in an efficient manner. I urge hon. members to show their support for these efforts by giving farmers this needed legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on the Farm Credit Act. We in this party were prepared to have this bill go through this evening. We agree the main thrust of this bill is the increase in money for loans. We were prepared to pass this piece of legislation quickly tonight. We wanted to see it go into committee, go through committee, and come back before the House dissolves, which I believe will not be too long.
Because the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) rose this evening and read a lot of statistics into the record, which everyone in Canada is aware of, and because he used up 20 minutes of the time of the House doing the job of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan)-

Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the House, which I failed to do in the first instance, of the fact that the Minister of Agriculture was performing another duty, and I was asked as Acting Minister of Agriculture to make a speech this evening. If the hon. member is going to say something which has never been heard in Canada before, we would be glad to hear it.

subtopic: PENSIONS-REQUESTED AMENDMENT TO LEGISLATION TO PROVIDE PENSIONS AT AGE 60 DESPITE MARITAL STATUS
PENSIONS-REQUESTED AMENDMENT TO LEGISLATION TO PROVIDE PENSIONS AT AGE 60 DESPITE MARITAL STATUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday, January 31, as recorded in Hansard at page 2387, I put this question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare? Now that she has been the head of her very important department long enough to know that a great many Canadian women between 60 and 65 feel very unhappy and upset over the fact that there is no pension for them unless they have the status of being married to and living with someone who is 65 or over, is the minister giving consideration to the necessary amendments to the Old Age Security Act so that persons between the ages of 60 and 65, particularly women, who are in need will get a pension without regard to their marital status?
The reply of the minister was in these words:
Mr. Speaker, I answered the same question very recently put to me by other members of this House. We are reviewing the situation, and I have nothing new to add today. As soon as I am ready to give a further explanation, I will do so.
In today's atmosphere I feel like saying: "This is where I came in". My reference to today's atmosphere, is, of course, to the fact that everyone is thinking about the next election. I am

April 6, 1978

reminded of the fact that during the 1974 election I happened to be in my room late at night when the first news came over the television to the effect that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had indicated that day that if the Liberals were re-elected they would bring in a bill providing for what was to be known as the "spouse's allowance".
I remember that the Prime Minister in the announcement had said they were going through with this program because it would provide help to certain people, even though it would create certain problems. I said to myself: "How right the Prime Minister is". Once you start paying a pension to persons in any age bracket based on marital status you are creating as many problems as you solve. I know that the spouse's allowance is regarded by the government as one of those examples of equality because it is available to the younger spouse where the older spouse is 65 or over and is receiving the old age pension, regardless of whether the younger spouse is a husband or a wife.
The fact is that in most cases the spouse's allowance is granted to women. The government refuses to give us the exact statistics. It tells us it does not keep statistics on the basis of sex. In my experience I have had scores of letters from women complaining about the situation, particularly from women whose husbands have died, and I have not had one letter in the years this has been on the statute books from a man between 60 and 65 complaining that he does not get the benefit of this legislation. For all practical purposes the spouse's allowance is a piece of legislation for women.
In addition to the age requirement and the means test there is this marital test: you get this allowance as a woman only if you have a man. That is no test, Mr. Speaker, to be in any legislation today, particularly in days when we believe in equal rights. My plea to the government is that it correct the mistake soon that was made in that legislation and remove from it the marital test.
I do not like means or income tests, but I will accept a means test, an income test, or a work test and so on between 60 and 65 rather than a marital test.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), in some of her responses to me on this matter, has said that she is concerned not only for those between 60 and 65 but for those between 55 and 65 and for other categories as well. I commend her for that. She knows how warmly I commended her just the other day for that tremendous speech she made in Sherbrooke on March 13. It is one of the best speeches I have read for a long time.
However, Mr. Speaker, the whole thrust of what she is trying to do is defeated by a piece of legislation that says to women: "You get what you need, or what you should have, only on the basis of your attachment to a man". This marital test ought to be removed. Just as soon as possible there should be a pension available between 60 and 65, or between 55 and 65 if the government wants it that way, based on other tests if you will, but not on a marital test. I do hope that the problem
Adjournment Debate
that the Prime Minister realized four years ago would arise will be resolved by establishing a pension or an allowance in this younger age bracket based on need, if the government wants it that way, but based on the rights of people as individuals and not because of marital status.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Kenneth Robinson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PENSIONS-REQUESTED AMENDMENT TO LEGISLATION TO PROVIDE PENSIONS AT AGE 60 DESPITE MARITAL STATUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has raised again his usual question about the spouse's allowance program, and he has waxed very eloquent, as he usually does. I thank him also for the comments he has made about the minister and her concerns regarding senior citizens in particular, which is the topic we are discussing this evening.
The program with regard to the spouse's allowance was introduced to cover a specific situation-that faced by many married couples with little or no other income who are trying to get by on a single old age security pension. It is considered appropriate to use spouse's allowance for cases like this because the married couple already has a connection with the old age security program through the one spouse who has reached retirement age. Because it was designed for this specific requirement, the spouse's allowance was not made applicable in the case of widows, divorced persons, and other single people in the 60 to 64 year range.
It is recognized that many people in this age group also have need for income-assistance, but it should be remembered that these needs can be met through other programs such as provincial assistance programs which the government of Canada shares in under the provisions of the Canada Assistance Plan.
The idea of an income tested retirement benefit akin to the spouse's allowance which would be available to anyone in the 60 to 64 age group who needed it is an attractive idea. At this period of time, however, when it is particularly important to exercise restraint in government spending, one should look very carefully at the potential costs of such a program. A rough estimate indicates that introducing the proposed program would cost an additional amount in excess of $600 million annually. This estimate does not take into account the potential effect on the behaviour of people. That is, if people were encouraged to retire earlier because of the existence of such a benefit, then clearly the additional cost would be higher.
We would also have to ask ourselves whether the creation of such a program would lead to the adoption of age 60 as the normal retirement age in Canada, and whether we could afford such a development. It is a well known fact that when federal retirement benefits became available at age 65, that age soon became generally regarded as the normal age of retirement in the country.
Notwithstanding this question, the government has considered such a program in the past and will no doubt consider it again when economic circumstances make it feasible. The government will be continuing to examine other potential improvements in programs to assist people. In this context the

April 6, 1978
Adjournment Debate
government is looking at potential initiatives for supplementing income for those who work at inadequate levels of income, and there will be a continuing examination with the provinces regarding possible improvements to the income support system.
In conclusion, potential improvements to the system can and will be examined in the future. In the meantime it should be recognized that we do have programs to meet the income needs of people, and in particular the spouse's allowance is doing a good job of meeting the special need for which it was designed.

subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-GRANTS TO PLANNED PARENTHOOD FEDERATION
HEALTH AND WELFARE-GRANTS TO PLANNED PARENTHOOD FEDERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Monday I rose to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) the following question:
The chairperson of the allocations committee of the Planned Parenthood Federation said in her report of June 17, 1977:
It is important for associations to remember that their primary role is to be agents for change rather than service agencies.
Since the federation receives about $670,000 annually from the federal government, most of it from the minister's department, I aslc the minister whether she, as the principal financial supporter of that organization, endorses that statement?
I should like to put on the record the last part of the minister's reply, in which she said:
I can see the implications he-
Meaning me, the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock.
-is suggesting, and I do not think that is an honest, intellectual way to work. First of all, I should like to read the report; secondly, if the hon. member has clear allegations I would prefer that he had the guts to announce them.
I think that last part of her response does not deserve comment, Mr. Speaker, and so I shall refrain. Up to this point I have had considerable regard for the minister. But I am concerned about the first part of her answer where she said:
I do not see what is wrong with the statement, taken out of context, that the hon. member read to me.
That answer, Mr. Speaker, disturbs me a great deal. I am really not talking about whether the Planned Parenthood Association ought to exist or even whether the federal government ought to be supporting it financially. What I am talking about is to what extent the government and ministers of the government will permit our people to be free and independent determinants of their future, their lifestyle and what kind of people they choose to be. That really is the critical question. When any group says it is here to be an agent for change and is supported by taxpayers' dollars, I am concerned.
The minister is right. This statement made by the group does raise serious implications. Let us admit it, Mr. Speaker, we are living in a very pluralistic society. There are many different views of man and of life. The planned parenthood group apparently sees life from a very rationalistic and materi-

alistic point of view. Other groups such as the pro-life group see man as being a sacred person. There are other religions who see all life as being sacred, whether it is man, animal or insect. We live in a pluralistic society.
If the minister says she agrees that this agency ought to be an agent for change, my question is: How far is she willing to go to apply pressure to bring about a change of attitude? How much are the people going to have to change their convictions to conform to those agents of change? What if they do not want change? What if they want to maintain the convictions and lifestyle they have chosen for themselves? How far is the minister willing to go and to what extent is she willing to use taxpayers' money to bring about that change and try and convince people that they ought to change?
Within a rationalistic and materialistic view of life there are many different views, a whole range. Should there be such things as abortion on demand? What about abortion for those whom some invisible agency deems are not fit to raise a family, are not capable of raising a family? Should there be compulsory abortion? What about euthanasia and to whom should euthanasia apply? Should it only be for the elderly? At what point should we apply euthanasia for the elderly? What about euthanasia for the disabled who are "a burden" on society? At what point do we apply euthanasia if we are going to take a rationalistic view of life?
I come back to the question, Mr. Speaker: How far should any group in society be supported by the taxpayers' money to try to change people? That is the most sacred question. The most sacred faculty we have is the faculty of choice. If this is taken away from us by any means at all, we become dehumanized. We become animals. We do not have to go back very far in history to see examples of that.
The goal stated by this group raises ominous implications for this very sacred faculty which is ours by right. Furthermore, the government is elected to represent all Canadians. What about the other groups who disagree with that point of view? Are they not entitled to support? If the government is going to support planned parenthood, a group that thinks they are agents for change, what about the other groups in society who want to change society in a different way? Are they not entitled to taxpayers' dollars? Is the government going to represent only one small segment of society and the one very narrow view that it has chosen as being the right view for all people? How far is the government willing to make this choice for all Canadians?
I say again, Mr. Speaker, that the minister has chosen a very serious approach if she agrees, as she says she does, with the view that the planned parenthood group has espoused for itself. They ought to remember they are not simply there to be social servants, but they are to be agents of change.
I would like the parliamentary secretary to give me a clear indication of just how far the minister is willing to go to change society according to the norms that she has chosen for all of us, or that this group has chosen for us. How much
April 6, 1978

money are they willing to continue to spend? Will they be free and democratic enough to support other groups who might not agree with this particular group?

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Kenneth Robinson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-GRANTS TO PLANNED PARENTHOOD FEDERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have now had the opportunity to read the report of the allocations committee of the Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada for 1976-77. It was from the document I understand the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) quoted from when he asked his question on April 3. In it, the chairperson of the allocations committee reports on a meeting held June 17 at which several topics of relevance to the financial health of this national voluntary association were discussed. The report in its financial affairs section indicated, as did the hon. member on Monday, and I quote from the report:
"It is important for associations to remember that their primary role is to be agents for change rather than service agencies".
What is implied here is the primary role of the Family Planning Federation of Canada, which can be conceived as education and promotion of responsible parenthood for all Canadians.
This sentence further implies that voluntary agencies in the social and educational sectors are not to be primarily responsible for the delivery of health, welfare and education services. I am sure the hon. member would agree provision of services is the primary responsibility of provincial and municipal governments in this country. Let me take this opportunity to commend the two national voluntary associations active in family planning, SERENA Canada and the Planned Parenthood Federation, for their educational and promotional efforts toward ensuring that Canadians have the number of children they want and when they want them.
At the same time let me sketch the policy of the department on sustaining grants to national voluntary associations such as SERENA Canada and the Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada. These grants are made on a year-to-year basis, after annual review. The sustaining grants to the two associations, namely $175,000 to SERENA and $600,000 to the Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada, are calculated on the basis of their relative scope of activity in the country.
The sustaining grants have not increased over the last four years. Notice has been given that the department is attempting to reduce the dependence of the two organizations on federal funds. In other words, we have been working toward a pattern of financing in which the affiliates of the two associations will cease to be dependent upon the national organizations. We visualize the national offices being in receipt of revenue from their affiliates. This model is the typical pattern of funding for the voluntary sector in Canada. In the family planning field we do realize, however, that a number of years may pass before it can be fully implemented without loss of valuable educational and promotional effort.
Adjournment Debate
It is my firm belief that the voluntary sector's advocacy for social change has been influential in the development of the broad range of social services across Canada.

Mr. Speaker, on Monday of this week I asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) about a report from the London Conference over the weekend to Mr. R. Toombs, the senior energy adviser for the department. Mr. Toombs indicated some very real concerns about oil shortages in the next seven or eight years and called for a super conservation program. The minister indicated in his answer that this program, which included the possibility of rationing, would only be implemented in the case of an emergency.
According to the figures of the National Energy Board, this emergency is inevitable. A chart produced by the National Energy Board and a report on oil supply and demand made a year ago do not vary more than 50,000 barrels a day today, according to the department and the board. That report shows that in 1976 Canadians were producing two million barrels a day. By 1986, production will drop to one million barrels a day. This includes a growing amount that will come from the oil sands or tar sands.
In 1977 we had a deficiency of 17 per cent in our production. This will grow to 52 per cent by 1986. We were told in testimony recently that by that time oil will be $25 a barrel in today's dollars. Therefore, we will have a deficit of $10 billion.
The department's figures indicate additional supplies of gas and electricity will be coming on stream. However, by 1986, we can expect a 30 per cent deficit in our total energy needs. With a good conservation program, that can be reduced to 20 per cent. One problem is, there is no discernible program for crossing over. We are told that more supplies of gas are coming in, but the cross-over just is not there. We will run out of an extremely vital resource necessary to propel our automobiles and so on. There will not be the technology to use some of these other materials at an early date.
I say to the minister through the parliamentary secretary that a crisis situation is developing. A white paper should be produced at the earliest opportunity, if possible before this parliament dissolves, clearly setting the conservation alternatives before the public. It should set out the alternatives in terms of available technology to make the cross-over, the changes required in our automobiles, and much more drastic changes than have already been announced.
Changes in the price structure may bring about conservation. There may be a possible need for rationing almost immediately, well before we run out of oil. I believe that there is a global oil crisis. There will be shortages everywhere, not just in Canada, and we must anticipate these shortages. I believe it is essential that a white paper be produced so that Canadians can better understand prices and take part in the

April 6, 1978
Adjournment Debate
discussions which will decide how we must approach the super conservation program which is required.

speakeroldname: Mr. Frank Maine (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the question of the oil supply situation in Canada as foreseen for the next ten years, it can be noted that the country's production of conventional crude oil is forecast to decline from 1.4 million barrels a day in 1977 to the level of 900,000 barrels a day in the mid-1980's.
In order to minimize reliance on uncertain supplies of oil imports, this production would not only have to be supplemented by production of close to 200,000 barrels a day from the two oil sands projects now developed in the Athabasca oil sands, but also by a further production of 200,000 barrels a day from as yet undeveloped sources in the heavy oil areas and the oil sands, to provide for a total production of 1.3 billion barrels a day. Expected oil demands in 1985 will be over 2 million barrels a day, which indicates that between 700,000 and 800,000 barrels a day would have to be imported. This would be a minimum level of imports, in view of uncertainties regarding the timing of projects to bring on new heavy oil and oil sands sources.
The situation of extensive dependence on oil imports, to the extent of 800,000 barrels a day, raises two major concerns. Such a large reliance on oil imports would impact seriously on Canada's balance of payments position. Imports of 800,000 barrels a day would represent a drain on the country's balance of payments by some $6 billion in 1985, or possibly even more should the international price of oil escalate faster in the 1980's than now anticipated.
The second problem, one of even more significance, is the question of import dependence from a security of supply point of view. In the event of international oil supply restrictions or serious supply disruptions, the eastern part of Canada would be in a major deficit position after existing storage supplies were exhausted. In preparation for such an eventuality the government is considering several possibilities of developing underground oil storage facilities to lengthen the period in
which Canada could sustain itself in the event of an overseas supply curtailment. However, there are limits to storage development and, in any event, supply interruption would also be dealt with through some form of energy use curtailment.
To this end the government has developed an emergency preparedness plan which, in the event of a prolonged emergency, could be carried through to a rationing phase. The government has recognized that an emergency could occur at any time and, consequently, has actively been developing a preparedness plan since the occurrence of the 1973-74 Middle East crisis. This is a contingency plan to meet emergency circumstances. Other steps are being taken to reduce the dependence on overseas supplies in addition to the acceleration of oil resource development.
To reduce the gap between supply and demand as now projected for the mid-1980's, increasing emphasis is being placed on conservation measures. This includes measures to reduce energy use in the home, such as the Canadian home insulation program, measures to reduce gasoline and diesel oil consumption in transportation, and a number of programs to improve the efficiency of energy use in industry.
In summary, the government has prepared for the possible eventuality of international oil supply curtailment through the design of an emergency preparedness program. It is also taking steps to minimize the projected energy supply gap in the next decade through incentive policies designed to accelerate oil resource development and through conservation programs directed to the residential, transportation and industrial sectors. All these programs, whether for emergency conditions or to meet the normal problems of supply and demand, are part of the government's energy policy. The country's energy policy in this and other respects has been developed to respond to the circumstances of a dynamic and ever-changing international energy economy.
